/conditions/osteoarthritis.title: Osteoarthritis: Symptoms, Treatment & Exercises | UK
/conditions/osteoarthritis.description: UK guide to osteoarthritis: symptoms, diagnosis, NICE-recommended exercise, weight management, pain relief and when to see a GP.
/conditions/osteoarthritis.question: What is osteoarthritis?
/conditions/osteoarthritis.answer: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis in the UK. It happens when protective cartilage on the ends of your bones wears down over time, most often in knees, hips, hands and spine. Symptoms include joint pain that worsens with activity, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, swelling and reduced movement. It's manageable with exercise, weight control, and, when needed, medication or joint replacement.

faqs.q: Can osteoarthritis be reversed?
faqs.a: No, cartilage loss can't currently be reversed, but symptoms and progression can be significantly slowed with exercise, weight management and joint-friendly activity.

faqs.q: What's the best exercise for osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: Low-impact aerobic exercise (walking, cycling, swimming) plus strength training around the affected joint. NICE recommends 30 minutes most days.

faqs.q: Does osteoarthritis show on an X-ray?
faqs.a: Yes — X-rays show joint space narrowing and bone spurs, though symptoms don't always match imaging severity.

faqs.q: When should I see a GP?
faqs.a: If joint pain limits daily activity, wakes you at night, or hasn't improved after 6 weeks of self-management, book a GP appointment.

/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis.title: Rheumatoid Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis.description: UK guide to rheumatoid arthritis: early signs, symmetrical joint symptoms, DMARD treatment, diet support and living well with RA.
/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis.question: What is rheumatoid arthritis?
/conditions/rheumatoid-arthritis.answer: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the lining of your joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness — usually symmetrical (both hands, both feet). Early treatment with DMARDs (disease-modifying drugs) within 3 months of symptoms starting can prevent joint damage. It affects about 400,000 adults in the UK.

faqs.q: Is rheumatoid arthritis a disability?
faqs.a: It can qualify as a disability under the Equality Act 2010 if it substantially affects daily activities. Many people with RA are eligible for PIP.

faqs.q: What's the difference between OA and RA?
faqs.a: OA is wear-and-tear cartilage loss. RA is an autoimmune inflammatory disease. RA usually affects joints symmetrically and causes prolonged morning stiffness (>1 hour).

faqs.q: Can diet help RA?
faqs.a: A Mediterranean-style diet rich in oily fish, olive oil and vegetables can reduce inflammatory markers. It doesn't replace DMARDs but supports overall control.

/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis.title: Psoriatic Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis.description: UK guide to psoriatic arthritis: the link between psoriasis and joint inflammation, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment and self-care.
/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis.question: What is psoriatic arthritis?
/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis.answer: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is an inflammatory arthritis that affects around 1 in 5 people with psoriasis. It causes joint pain, swelling and stiffness — often in fingers, toes, lower back or knees — plus nail changes and skin plaques. Early diagnosis and DMARDs or biologics prevent joint damage.

faqs.q: Can you have PsA without psoriasis?
faqs.a: Yes, about 15% of people develop joint symptoms before skin symptoms. Family history and nail pitting are clues.

faqs.q: Is psoriatic arthritis worse than rheumatoid arthritis?
faqs.a: Both can cause serious joint damage. PsA has more variable patterns; RA is usually more symmetrical. Outcomes depend on early treatment.

/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis.title: Ankylosing Spondylitis (axSpA) | UK Guide
/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis.description: UK guide to ankylosing spondylitis: inflammatory back pain, morning stiffness, diagnosis, daily exercise, physio and biologic treatment.
/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis.question: What is ankylosing spondylitis?
/conditions/ankylosing-spondylitis.answer: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS), or axial spondyloarthritis, is a long-term inflammatory arthritis mainly affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints. It typically starts in the late teens or twenties with gradual lower back pain and morning stiffness that improves with movement. Daily exercise, physio and biologic drugs keep the spine flexible.

/conditions/gout.title: Gout: Causes, Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
/conditions/gout.description: UK guide to gout: uric acid crystals, sudden severe joint pain, allopurinol treatment after repeat attacks, diet and alcohol changes.
/conditions/gout.question: What is gout?
/conditions/gout.answer: Gout is a type of inflammatory arthritis caused by high uric acid crystallising inside joints — usually the big toe — triggering sudden severe pain, redness and swelling. UK guidelines recommend urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol) after a second attack to prevent joint damage. Diet and alcohol adjustments help.

/conditions/fibromyalgia.title: Fibromyalgia: Symptoms & Management | UK Guide
/conditions/fibromyalgia.description: UK guide to fibromyalgia: widespread pain, fatigue, fibro fog and sleep problems, plus NICE-recommended exercise, CBT and pacing.
/conditions/fibromyalgia.question: What is fibromyalgia?
/conditions/fibromyalgia.answer: Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition causing widespread pain, fatigue, sleep problems and 'fibro fog'. It's a disorder of pain processing rather than joint damage. NICE recommends graded exercise, CBT and paced activity as first-line management.

/conditions/lupus.title: Lupus (SLE): Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
/conditions/lupus.description: UK guide to lupus (SLE): joint pain, butterfly rash, fatigue and sun sensitivity, plus hydroxychloroquine treatment and self-care.
/conditions/lupus.question: What is lupus?
/conditions/lupus.answer: Lupus (systemic lupus erythematosus, SLE) is an autoimmune disease that can affect skin, joints, kidneys, heart and lungs. Common symptoms include joint pain, a butterfly rash, fatigue and sun sensitivity. Hydroxychloroquine is the mainstay of treatment.

/conditions/knee-arthritis.title: Knee Arthritis: Symptoms, Exercises & Relief | UK
/conditions/knee-arthritis.description: UK guide to knee arthritis: pain on stairs and walking, stiffness after rest, NICE first-line exercise, weight loss and treatment options.
/conditions/knee-arthritis.question: What is knee arthritis?
/conditions/knee-arthritis.answer: Knee arthritis is joint damage in the knee — most often osteoarthritis — causing pain when standing, walking or climbing stairs, stiffness after rest, and swelling. NICE recommends exercise and weight loss as first-line treatment; every 5 kg lost cuts knee load by roughly 20 kg.

faqs.q: What's the best exercise for knee arthritis?
faqs.a: Quadriceps strengthening (straight-leg raises, wall sits) plus low-impact aerobic (cycling, swimming). 3-5 sessions a week for 8+ weeks shows meaningful pain reduction.

faqs.q: Should I use a walking stick?
faqs.a: Use it in the opposite hand to the painful knee — this reduces load by up to 25%.

/conditions/hip-arthritis.title: Hip Arthritis: Symptoms, Exercises & Relief | UK
/conditions/hip-arthritis.description: UK guide to hip arthritis: groin and buttock pain, stiffness, physio-led strengthening, weight management and hip replacement options.
/conditions/hip-arthritis.question: What is hip arthritis?
/conditions/hip-arthritis.answer: Hip arthritis is joint damage — usually osteoarthritis — of the hip, causing groin or buttock pain, stiffness and difficulty putting on socks or shoes. Physio-led strengthening, weight management and, when severe, hip replacement (over 100,000 done in the UK each year) provide long-term relief.

/conditions/hand-arthritis.title: Hand Arthritis: Symptoms & Exercises | UK Guide
/conditions/hand-arthritis.description: UK guide to hand arthritis: finger, thumb and wrist symptoms of OA and RA, plus splints, hand exercises and topical NSAID gels.
/conditions/hand-arthritis.question: What is hand arthritis?
/conditions/hand-arthritis.answer: Hand arthritis affects the small joints of the fingers, thumbs and wrists. Osteoarthritis typically causes bony bumps and thumb-base pain; rheumatoid usually causes symmetrical knuckle swelling. Splints, hand exercises and topical NSAID gels help most people.

/conditions/shoulder-arthritis.title: Shoulder Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
/conditions/shoulder-arthritis.description: UK guide to shoulder arthritis: glenohumeral and AC joint OA, night pain, reduced reach, physio, injections and replacement options.
/conditions/shoulder-arthritis.question: What is shoulder arthritis?
/conditions/shoulder-arthritis.answer: Shoulder arthritis is cartilage loss in the glenohumeral or acromioclavicular joints, causing deep aching pain, reduced reach and night pain when lying on the affected side. Physio, corticosteroid injections and, if severe, shoulder replacement are options.

/conditions/elbow-arthritis.title: Elbow Arthritis: Symptoms & Treatment | UK Guide
/conditions/elbow-arthritis.description: UK guide to elbow arthritis: pain, stiffness, locking and grating in the elbow, with treatments from NSAIDs to arthroscopy and replacement.
/conditions/elbow-arthritis.question: What is elbow arthritis?
/conditions/elbow-arthritis.answer: Elbow arthritis is joint damage in the elbow causing pain, stiffness, locking or grating during movement. Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis are the main causes. Treatment ranges from activity modification and NSAIDs to arthroscopy or elbow replacement.

/conditions/juvenile-arthritis.title: Juvenile Arthritis (JIA) in Children | UK Guide
/conditions/juvenile-arthritis.description: UK guide to juvenile idiopathic arthritis: signs in children under 16, diagnosis, paediatric rheumatology care and DMARD treatment.
/conditions/juvenile-arthritis.question: What is juvenile arthritis?
/conditions/juvenile-arthritis.answer: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is arthritis starting before age 16, lasting more than 6 weeks. It affects around 1 in 1,000 UK children. Early paediatric rheumatology care and DMARDs help most children live active lives.

/conditions/reactive-arthritis.title: Reactive Arthritis: Causes & Recovery | UK Guide
/conditions/reactive-arthritis.description: UK guide to reactive arthritis: joint inflammation after gut or urinary infection, typical symptoms, treatment and recovery timeline.
/conditions/reactive-arthritis.question: What is reactive arthritis?
/conditions/reactive-arthritis.answer: Reactive arthritis is joint inflammation that develops after an infection elsewhere in the body — usually gut or urinary. Symptoms include joint pain, eye inflammation and urinary symptoms. Most cases resolve within 3-12 months.

/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica.title: Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR) | UK Guide
/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica.description: UK guide to polymyalgia rheumatica: sudden shoulder and hip stiffness over 50, low-dose steroid treatment and what recovery looks like.
/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica.question: What is polymyalgia rheumatica?
/conditions/polymyalgia-rheumatica.answer: Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) causes sudden shoulder and hip stiffness and pain, mainly in adults over 50. Low-dose steroids (prednisolone 15 mg) usually give dramatic relief within days. Treatment typically continues for 1-2 years.

/guides/newly-diagnosed.title: Newly Diagnosed With Arthritis? Start Here | UK
/guides/newly-diagnosed.description: Just diagnosed with arthritis? UK starter guide: rheumatology follow-up, gentle daily movement, symptom tracking and free physio triage.
/guides/newly-diagnosed.question: I've just been diagnosed with arthritis — what should I do?
/guides/newly-diagnosed.answer: Book a rheumatology follow-up if not already arranged, start gentle daily movement, and read up on your specific type. NICE recommends beginning exercise and joint protection within weeks of diagnosis for best long-term outcomes. Track symptoms, ask your GP about pain relief options, and consider our free virtual physiotherapy triage.

/guides/arthritis-pain-relief.title: Arthritis Pain Relief: What Works | UK Guide
/guides/arthritis-pain-relief.description: Evidence-based arthritis pain relief for UK patients: paracetamol, topical NSAID gels, heat and cold, exercise, injections and DMARDs.
/guides/arthritis-pain-relief.question: How do I relieve arthritis pain?
/guides/arthritis-pain-relief.answer: First-line pain relief includes paracetamol, topical NSAID gels and heat/cold packs. Exercise reduces pain more than most drugs long-term. If pain persists, your GP can consider oral NSAIDs, corticosteroid injections or, for inflammatory arthritis, DMARDs.

/guides/hip-exercises-for-osteoarthritis.title: Best Hip Exercises for Osteoarthritis | UK Guide
/guides/hip-exercises-for-osteoarthritis.description: Evidence-based hip OA exercises: glute bridges, clamshells, hip abduction, wall squats and cycling — with NICE-aligned weekly targets.
/guides/hip-exercises-for-osteoarthritis.question: What are the best hip exercises for osteoarthritis?
/guides/hip-exercises-for-osteoarthritis.answer: Evidence-based hip OA exercises include glute bridges, clamshells, standing hip abduction, wall squats and stationary cycling. Aim for 3 sessions per week of 30 minutes; expect meaningful pain reduction after 8-12 weeks. NICE guideline NG226 recommends supervised programmes.

/guides/can-exercise-make-osteoarthritis.title: Can Exercise Make Osteoarthritis Worse? | UK Guide
/guides/can-exercise-make-osteoarthritis.description: Worried exercise will damage arthritic joints? What normal soreness looks like, warning signs of overdoing it, and how to progress safely.
/guides/can-exercise-make-osteoarthritis.question: Can exercise make osteoarthritis worse?
/guides/can-exercise-make-osteoarthritis.answer: No — done correctly, exercise reduces OA pain and slows progression. Some soreness during and up to 2 hours after exercise is normal. Sharp, sudden or persistent pain lasting more than 24 hours means you've done too much; scale back but don't stop.

/guides/fall-prevention-older-adults.title: Fall Prevention for Older Adults | UK Guide
/guides/fall-prevention-older-adults.description: How older adults can prevent falls: strength and balance training, home hazard checks, medication review, eye tests and vitamin D.
/guides/fall-prevention-older-adults.question: How can older adults prevent falls?
/guides/fall-prevention-older-adults.answer: Strength and balance training (tai chi, Otago programme) cuts falls by around 30%. Also: home hazard checks, medication review, eye tests every 2 years and vitamin D 10 mcg/day. Contact your GP or NHS falls clinic if you've fallen twice in a year.

/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-control.title: Sarcopenia: Rebuilding Muscle After 60 | UK Guide
/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-control.description: UK guide to sarcopenia: why age-related muscle loss worsens arthritis, and how resistance training and protein intake can reverse it.
/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-control.question: What is sarcopenia?
/guides/sarcopenia-muscle-control.answer: Sarcopenia is age-related muscle loss that accelerates after 60 and worsens arthritis symptoms. Resistance training (2-3 sessions per week) plus 1.0-1.2 g protein/kg body weight/day reverses much of it, even in your 80s.

/guides/bone-density-osteoporosis.title: Improving Bone Density & Osteoporosis | UK Guide
/guides/bone-density-osteoporosis.description: How to improve bone density in the UK: weight-bearing exercise, resistance training, calcium and vitamin D, FRAX scores and treatment.
/guides/bone-density-osteoporosis.question: How do I improve bone density?
/guides/bone-density-osteoporosis.answer: Weight-bearing exercise (walking, jogging, dancing), resistance training, calcium 700 mg/day and vitamin D 10 mcg/day support bone density. If your FRAX score is high, your GP may prescribe bisphosphonates.

/guides/disability-support.title: UK Disability Support for Arthritis | Guide
/guides/disability-support.description: UK disability support for arthritis: PIP, Blue Badge, Access to Work grants, workplace adjustments and where to get application help.
/guides/disability-support.question: What UK disability support is available for arthritis?
/guides/disability-support.answer: You may qualify for Personal Independence Payment (PIP), Blue Badge, Access to Work grants, and workplace reasonable adjustments under the Equality Act 2010. Citizens Advice and Versus Arthritis helpline (0800 5200 520) guide applications.

/guides/frailty-management-hub.title: Frailty Management With Arthritis | UK Guide
/guides/frailty-management-hub.description: Managing frailty alongside arthritis: strength training, protein-rich diet, medication review, sensory checks and GP frailty assessment.
/guides/frailty-management-hub.question: How is frailty managed with arthritis?
/guides/frailty-management-hub.answer: Frailty and arthritis together respond to comprehensive geriatric assessment: strength training, protein-rich diet, medication review, hearing/vision checks and social connection. Ask your GP for a formal frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale) review.

/guides/preventative-msk-health.title: Preventative Muscle & Joint Health | UK Guide
/guides/preventative-msk-health.description: Keep muscles and joints healthy for life: weekly activity targets, strength sessions, sleep, Mediterranean diet and weight guidance.
/guides/preventative-msk-health.question: How do I keep my muscles and joints healthy?
/guides/preventative-msk-health.answer: The three pillars are: 150 minutes moderate aerobic activity per week, 2 strength sessions per week, and 7-9 hours of sleep. Add Mediterranean-style diet, don't smoke, and keep BMI under 27 for lowest lifetime arthritis risk.

/guides/musculoskeletal-health.title: Musculoskeletal (MSK) Health Explained | UK
/guides/musculoskeletal-health.description: What musculoskeletal health means, why MSK conditions affect 20 million people in the UK, and the four proven levers that protect it.
/guides/musculoskeletal-health.question: What is musculoskeletal health?
/guides/musculoskeletal-health.answer: Musculoskeletal (MSK) health means healthy bones, joints, muscles, tendons and ligaments. MSK conditions affect 20 million people in the UK. Movement, strength, sleep and weight management are the four proven levers to protect it.

/diet-hub.title: Diet & Nutrition Hub for Arthritis | UK
/diet-hub.description: The best diet for arthritis: Mediterranean eating, anti-inflammatory foods, weight loss guidance and UK supermarket-friendly meal plans.
/diet-hub.question: What's the best diet for arthritis?
/diet-hub.answer: A Mediterranean diet — oily fish twice a week, olive oil, nuts, wholegrains, plenty of vegetables and fruit — consistently reduces inflammation markers and joint pain in trials. Cut ultra-processed foods, sugary drinks and excess red meat. Weight loss of 5-10% substantially reduces knee OA pain.

/exercise-hub.title: Exercise Hub: Arthritis-Friendly Workouts | UK
/exercise-hub.description: Free arthritis exercise hub: aerobic, strength and flexibility routines by joint, NICE-aligned plans and short home video sessions.
/exercise-hub.question: What's the best exercise for arthritis?
/exercise-hub.answer: Combine aerobic (walking, swimming, cycling) with strength training 2-3 times a week and flexibility work. NICE guideline NG226 recommends exercise as first-line for all arthritis types — with pain reduction comparable to NSAIDs and no side effects.

/arthritis-support/london.title: Arthritis Support in London | Free UK Guide
/arthritis-support/london.description: Free arthritis support for people in London: NHS physio self-referral, local rheumatology at London Rheumatology, NHS trusts across all boroughs, exercise classes, and benefits help.
/arthritis-support/london.question: Where can I find arthritis support in London?
/arthritis-support/london.answer: Living With Arthritis UK is a national charity supporting people with arthritis across the UK, including those in London and the surrounding area. If you live in London and are managing joint pain, our free, NICE-aligned guides on exercise, anti-inflammatory diet, pain relief and NHS self-referral routes are available online. For local NHS care, London is served by London Rheumatology, NHS trusts across all boroughs, which provides rheumatology and musculoskeletal (MSK) services — you can usually access physiotherapy through NHS self-referral without a GP appointment.

faqs.q: How do I access NHS physiotherapy in London?
faqs.a: Most parts of London allow direct self-referral to NHS MSK physiotherapy — search 'NHS physiotherapy self referral London' or ask your GP practice. Waiting times vary but are typically 4-12 weeks; our Exercise Hub offers evidence-based routines you can start immediately.

faqs.q: Are there free arthritis exercise classes in London?
faqs.a: London usually has options through NHS falls-prevention programmes, local council leisure schemes, Age UK, and Versus Arthritis groups. Search 'London strength and balance class' or 'London tai chi for arthritis' — your GP practice or local library often maintain lists. Our online Tai Chi hub is free and joint-friendly if travelling is difficult.

faqs.q: How do I claim PIP for arthritis if I live in London?
faqs.a: PIP claims work the same across England, Wales and Northern Ireland (Scotland uses Adult Disability Payment). Your local Citizens Advice office in London offers free application help. Read our benefits guide for a step-by-step overview.

/guides/paracetamol-vs-ibuprofen-for-art.title: Paracetamol vs Ibuprofen for Arthritis Pain
/guides/paracetamol-vs-ibuprofen-for-art.description: For arthritis pain in UK adults, NICE recommends topical NSAID gels (like ibuprofen gel) first for hand and knee OA. Oral paracetamol is a reasonable short-t...
/guides/paracetamol-vs-ibuprofen-for-art.breadcrumb: Paracetamol vs Ibuprofen for Arthritis Pain
/guides/paracetamol-vs-ibuprofen-for-art.question: Should I take paracetamol or ibuprofen for arthritis pain?
/guides/paracetamol-vs-ibuprofen-for-art.answer: For arthritis pain in UK adults, NICE recommends topical NSAID gels (like ibuprofen gel) first for hand and knee OA. Oral paracetamol is a reasonable short-term option but the evidence for its benefit in OA is weaker than once thought. Oral ibuprofen works better for inflammation but carries stomach, kidney and heart risks — take it with food, at the lowest effective dose, for the shortest time, and check with your GP if you're over 65, on blood pressure medication, or have kidney or heart conditions.

faqs.q: When would you pick Paracetamol?
faqs.a: Occasional mild pain; can't tolerate NSAIDs; on blood thinners.

faqs.q: When would you pick Ibuprofen (oral NSAID)?
faqs.a: Inflammation-driven pain (RA, gout, PsA flares); short-term use only.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Neither replaces exercise, weight management or DMARDs for inflammatory arthritis. Never combine oral NSAIDs with aspirin without medical advice.

/guides/topical-nsaid-vs-oral-nsaid-arth.title: Topical NSAID Gel vs Oral NSAID: Which Is Safer?
/guides/topical-nsaid-vs-oral-nsaid-arth.description: For knee and hand osteoarthritis, NICE now recommends topical NSAID gels as first-line — they work almost as well as oral NSAIDs for pain but with a fraction...
/guides/topical-nsaid-vs-oral-nsaid-arth.breadcrumb: Topical NSAID Gel vs Oral NSAID: Which Is Safer?
/guides/topical-nsaid-vs-oral-nsaid-arth.question: Is topical ibuprofen gel as good as oral ibuprofen for arthritis?
/guides/topical-nsaid-vs-oral-nsaid-arth.answer: For knee and hand osteoarthritis, NICE now recommends topical NSAID gels as first-line — they work almost as well as oral NSAIDs for pain but with a fraction of the stomach, kidney and cardiovascular risk. Oral NSAIDs remain useful for deep joints (hip, spine) or widespread inflammation but should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time.

faqs.q: When would you pick Topical NSAID gel?
faqs.a: Hand or knee OA; localised joint pain; older adults; anyone on multiple medications.

faqs.q: When would you pick Oral NSAID (tablets)?
faqs.a: Hip/spine OA; inflammatory arthritis flares; short bursts under GP supervision.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Topical NSAIDs still carry a small systemic absorption risk — avoid on broken skin and follow the pack instructions.

/guides/physiotherapy-vs-surgery-knee-ar.title: Physiotherapy vs Surgery for Knee Arthritis
/guides/physiotherapy-vs-surgery-knee-ar.description: NICE requires that all people with knee OA are offered a structured exercise and physio programme first — surgery (partial or total knee replacement) is a la...
/guides/physiotherapy-vs-surgery-knee-ar.breadcrumb: Physiotherapy vs Surgery for Knee Arthritis
/guides/physiotherapy-vs-surgery-knee-ar.question: Should I have physio or knee surgery for arthritis?
/guides/physiotherapy-vs-surgery-knee-ar.answer: NICE requires that all people with knee OA are offered a structured exercise and physio programme first — surgery (partial or total knee replacement) is a last-resort option when pain and function haven't improved despite consistent physio, weight management, and pain relief. Around 100,000 knee replacements are done in the UK each year, and outcomes are best for those who've maintained muscle strength through physio beforehand.

faqs.q: When would you pick Physiotherapy-led exercise programme?
faqs.a: First-line for everyone with knee OA; before considering surgery; for maintenance long-term.

faqs.q: When would you pick Knee replacement surgery?
faqs.a: Severe daily pain despite 12+ weeks of physio; night pain that disturbs sleep; imaging shows advanced bone-on-bone changes.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Even after surgery, physiotherapy is essential for recovery — muscle strength before surgery predicts recovery speed.

/guides/nhs-vs-private-rheumatology.title: NHS vs Private Rheumatology in the UK
/guides/nhs-vs-private-rheumatology.description: NHS rheumatology provides the same specialist care and drugs as private, at no cost — but waiting times for a first appointment can be 12-30 weeks. Private c...
/guides/nhs-vs-private-rheumatology.breadcrumb: NHS vs Private Rheumatology in the UK
/guides/nhs-vs-private-rheumatology.question: Should I go private for arthritis care in the UK?
/guides/nhs-vs-private-rheumatology.answer: NHS rheumatology provides the same specialist care and drugs as private, at no cost — but waiting times for a first appointment can be 12-30 weeks. Private consultations (£150-300) get you seen within days, but ongoing NHS care is usually still the destination for DMARDs and biologics because private prescriptions are expensive. A common practical route: private consultation to get diagnosed and started faster, then transfer to NHS for long-term treatment.

faqs.q: When would you pick NHS rheumatology?
faqs.a: Long-term treatment; DMARDs and biologics (very expensive privately); ongoing follow-up.

faqs.q: When would you pick Private rheumatology?
faqs.a: Urgent diagnosis; second opinion; you can't wait 3-6 months for a first appointment.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Ask any private consultant whether they also work in the NHS — many do, and this makes NHS transfer smoother.

/guides/swimming-vs-walking-arthritis.title: Swimming vs Walking for Arthritis
/guides/swimming-vs-walking-arthritis.description: Both are excellent, but they target different needs. Swimming and aqua aerobics remove weight from joints, making them ideal for severe knee/hip pain, flares...
/guides/swimming-vs-walking-arthritis.question: Is swimming or walking better for arthritis?
/guides/swimming-vs-walking-arthritis.answer: Both are excellent, but they target different needs. Swimming and aqua aerobics remove weight from joints, making them ideal for severe knee/hip pain, flares, or people who can't walk far. Walking is weight-bearing (better for bone density), free, and easier to fit into daily life. Most rheumatologists recommend both: walking daily for cardiovascular and bone health, swimming 1-2x/week for joint relief.

faqs.q: When would you pick Swimming / aqua aerobics?
faqs.a: Severe knee or hip OA; flares; obesity; loss of confidence; heat helps your joints.

faqs.q: When would you pick Walking?
faqs.a: Bone density (weight-bearing); daily habit; mild to moderate arthritis; free.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Cold pools can trigger some conditions (Raynaud's, fibromyalgia) — look for a heated pool.

/guides/yoga-vs-pilates-arthritis.title: Yoga vs Pilates for Arthritis
/guides/yoga-vs-pilates-arthritis.description: Both improve mobility and pain, but Pilates is generally easier to modify for arthritis because it emphasises controlled, low-range movement and core strengt...
/guides/yoga-vs-pilates-arthritis.question: Should I try yoga or Pilates for arthritis?
/guides/yoga-vs-pilates-arthritis.answer: Both improve mobility and pain, but Pilates is generally easier to modify for arthritis because it emphasises controlled, low-range movement and core strength. Yoga is more varied — 'gentle', 'chair' or 'restorative' yoga are arthritis-friendly, but avoid Ashtanga, hot yoga, and any deep joint-loading poses. Look for an instructor with disability or older-adult experience.

faqs.q: When would you pick Pilates (mat or reformer)?
faqs.a: Core weakness; back pain; want measured, controlled progression.

faqs.q: When would you pick Yoga (gentle/chair/restorative)?
faqs.a: Stiffness; stress and mood benefits; balance work; enjoy mindfulness.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Skip any class that pushes 'no pain no gain' — arthritis-friendly practice should never sharply hurt.

/guides/glucosamine-vs-turmeric-arthriti.title: Glucosamine vs Turmeric for Arthritis
/guides/glucosamine-vs-turmeric-arthriti.description: The evidence for both is mixed. Glucosamine (with chondroitin) has modest benefit for some people with knee OA over 6+ months of use, but many trials show no...
/guides/glucosamine-vs-turmeric-arthriti.question: Does glucosamine or turmeric work better for arthritis?
/guides/glucosamine-vs-turmeric-arthriti.answer: The evidence for both is mixed. Glucosamine (with chondroitin) has modest benefit for some people with knee OA over 6+ months of use, but many trials show no effect. Turmeric (curcumin) shows more consistent anti-inflammatory effect in trials, with fewer safety concerns for most people. Neither is a substitute for exercise, weight management or prescribed medication.

faqs.q: When would you pick Glucosamine + chondroitin?
faqs.a: Knee OA; willing to try for 3-6 months; can afford £15-30/month.

faqs.q: When would you pick Turmeric / curcumin?
faqs.a: Inflammatory-type pain; wanting an anti-inflammatory food/supplement.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Turmeric can interact with blood thinners. Speak to your pharmacist if you take warfarin, DOACs or diabetes medication.

/guides/heat-vs-cold-arthritis-pain.title: Heat vs Cold Therapy for Arthritis
/guides/heat-vs-cold-arthritis-pain.description: Use heat for stiff, aching joints (typical morning OA symptoms, general muscle tension) — it relaxes tissue and boosts blood flow. Use cold for acutely infla...
/guides/heat-vs-cold-arthritis-pain.breadcrumb: Heat vs Cold Therapy for Arthritis
/guides/heat-vs-cold-arthritis-pain.question: Should I use a heat pad or ice pack for arthritis?
/guides/heat-vs-cold-arthritis-pain.answer: Use heat for stiff, aching joints (typical morning OA symptoms, general muscle tension) — it relaxes tissue and boosts blood flow. Use cold for acutely inflamed, swollen joints (gout attacks, RA flares, after over-doing exercise) — it reduces swelling and dulls pain. Both are safe, cheap and evidence-supported. Apply for 15-20 minutes with a cloth barrier.

faqs.q: When would you pick Heat (heat pad, warm bath, wheat bag)?
faqs.a: Morning stiffness; ongoing dull ache; before exercise; muscle tension around a joint.

faqs.q: When would you pick Cold (ice pack, frozen peas in a cloth)?
faqs.a: Acute flare or gout attack; visibly swollen joint; after over-exertion.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Never apply either directly to skin — always use a cloth or towel barrier.

/guides/walking-stick-vs-crutch-arthriti.title: Walking Stick vs Crutch for Arthritis
/guides/walking-stick-vs-crutch-arthriti.description: For arthritis in one hip or knee, a walking stick in the OPPOSITE hand reduces joint load by up to 25% — this is the standard NHS/physio recommendation. Crut...
/guides/walking-stick-vs-crutch-arthriti.breadcrumb: Walking Stick vs Crutch for Arthritis
/guides/walking-stick-vs-crutch-arthriti.question: Do I need a walking stick or a crutch?
/guides/walking-stick-vs-crutch-arthriti.answer: For arthritis in one hip or knee, a walking stick in the OPPOSITE hand reduces joint load by up to 25% — this is the standard NHS/physio recommendation. Crutches (elbow crutches usually) are for temporary post-surgery use or for people with weakness or balance issues affecting both legs. Get sized properly: the handle should reach your wrist when you stand with your arms by your sides.

faqs.q: When would you pick Walking stick (single)?
faqs.a: Osteoarthritis in one knee or hip; occasional support; balance help.

faqs.q: When would you pick Elbow crutches?
faqs.a: Post-op recovery; bilateral weakness; when a stick doesn't give enough support.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: See a physiotherapist for correct sizing and gait — bad technique makes joint pain worse, not better.

/guides/rollator-vs-walking-frame.title: Rollator vs Walking Frame (Zimmer): Which Should You Choose?
/guides/rollator-vs-walking-frame.description: A rollator (wheeled walker with brakes and a seat) is best for people who can walk short-medium distances but need support and rest — most arthritis, elderly...
/guides/rollator-vs-walking-frame.breadcrumb: Rollator vs Walking Frame (Zimmer): Which Should You Choose?
/guides/rollator-vs-walking-frame.question: Should I use a rollator or a walking frame?
/guides/rollator-vs-walking-frame.answer: A rollator (wheeled walker with brakes and a seat) is best for people who can walk short-medium distances but need support and rest — most arthritis, elderly and MSK conditions. A traditional walking frame (Zimmer) is better for people who need maximum stability and don't need to travel far — usually indoors, after surgery, or with severe balance issues.

faqs.q: When would you pick Rollator (4-wheel, brakes, seat)?
faqs.a: Community mobility; longer walks; you want to sit and rest; outdoor use.

faqs.q: When would you pick Walking frame (Zimmer)?
faqs.a: Post-op stability; indoors only; severe balance issues; falls risk.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: NHS occupational therapy can assess you at home and provide the right aid free of charge — ask your GP for a referral.

/guides/dmards-vs-biologics.title: DMARDs vs Biologics for Rheumatoid Arthritis
/guides/dmards-vs-biologics.description: Conventional DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide) are the first-line drugs for RA and other inflammatory arthritis — cheap, ...
/guides/dmards-vs-biologics.breadcrumb: DMARDs vs Biologics for Rheumatoid Arthritis
/guides/dmards-vs-biologics.question: What's the difference between DMARDs and biologics?
/guides/dmards-vs-biologics.answer: Conventional DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide) are the first-line drugs for RA and other inflammatory arthritis — cheap, taken by mouth, and effective for the majority of people. Biologics (adalimumab, etanercept, tocilizumab and others) are injected or infused, target specific parts of the immune system, and are added when DMARDs alone aren't enough. NHS NICE guidance sets clear criteria for stepping up.

faqs.q: When would you pick Conventional DMARDs (e.g. methotrexate)?
faqs.a: First-line for RA, PsA, some other inflammatory arthritis; NICE requires trying these first.

faqs.q: When would you pick Biologics (e.g. adalimumab, etanercept)?
faqs.a: When DMARDs alone don't achieve remission (usually after 3-6 months of adequate dose).

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Both need regular blood monitoring. Never stop suddenly without medical advice — flare risk.

/guides/steroid-injection-vs-hyaluronic-.title: Steroid Injection vs Hyaluronic Acid for Knee Arthritis
/guides/steroid-injection-vs-hyaluronic-.description: Steroid (corticosteroid) injections give faster, more consistent pain relief but the effect only lasts 4-12 weeks and repeated use can accelerate joint damag...
/guides/steroid-injection-vs-hyaluronic-.breadcrumb: Steroid Injection vs Hyaluronic Acid for Knee Arthritis
/guides/steroid-injection-vs-hyaluronic-.question: Should I have a steroid or hyaluronic acid injection in my knee?
/guides/steroid-injection-vs-hyaluronic-.answer: Steroid (corticosteroid) injections give faster, more consistent pain relief but the effect only lasts 4-12 weeks and repeated use can accelerate joint damage — the NHS typically limits them to 3-4 per year. Hyaluronic acid injections work more slowly but effects can last 6 months; NICE has moved away from routinely recommending them because evidence is mixed, and they're rarely offered on the NHS.

faqs.q: When would you pick Corticosteroid injection?
faqs.a: Acute flare; wanting fast relief; short-term bridge to physio or surgery.

faqs.q: When would you pick Hyaluronic acid injection?
faqs.a: You want longer-lasting relief and can access it privately (£250-500 per injection).

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Neither treats the underlying arthritis — pair with exercise and weight management.

/guides/gout-vs-pseudogout.title: Gout vs Pseudogout: What's the Difference?
/guides/gout-vs-pseudogout.description: Both cause sudden, severe joint pain and swelling from crystals in the joint, but the crystals and typical targets differ. Gout (uric acid crystals) most oft...
/guides/gout-vs-pseudogout.breadcrumb: Gout vs Pseudogout: What's the Difference?
/guides/gout-vs-pseudogout.question: How do I tell gout and pseudogout apart?
/guides/gout-vs-pseudogout.answer: Both cause sudden, severe joint pain and swelling from crystals in the joint, but the crystals and typical targets differ. Gout (uric acid crystals) most often hits the big toe, is linked to diet and alcohol, and is treated by lowering uric acid (allopurinol). Pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate crystals) usually hits the knee or wrist, is more common in older adults, and isn't diet-linked — treatment focuses on managing flares.

faqs.q: When would you pick Gout (uric acid)?
faqs.a: Big toe, ankle or knee; often at night; alcohol/rich food trigger; family history.

faqs.q: When would you pick Pseudogout (CPPD)?
faqs.a: Knee or wrist; over 60; no diet trigger; sometimes triggered by illness or surgery.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: The only way to be certain is joint aspiration — a needle sample examined under a microscope for crystal type.

/guides/osteoarthritis-vs-rheumatoid-art.title: Osteoarthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis
/guides/osteoarthritis-vs-rheumatoid-art.description: Osteoarthritis (OA) is wear-and-tear cartilage loss — most common, usually one-sided or asymmetrical, pain worse with activity, morning stiffness under 30 mi...
/guides/osteoarthritis-vs-rheumatoid-art.question: What's the difference between osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis?
/guides/osteoarthritis-vs-rheumatoid-art.answer: Osteoarthritis (OA) is wear-and-tear cartilage loss — most common, usually one-sided or asymmetrical, pain worse with activity, morning stiffness under 30 minutes. Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is autoimmune — the immune system attacks joints, usually symmetrical (both hands, both feet), morning stiffness over an hour, plus fatigue. RA needs urgent rheumatology referral because early DMARDs prevent joint damage.

faqs.q: When would you pick Osteoarthritis (OA)?
faqs.a: Older, wear-related pattern; specific joints; activity-related; imaging shows joint space narrowing.

faqs.q: When would you pick Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)?
faqs.a: Symmetrical joint swelling; long morning stiffness; fatigue; blood tests show inflammation (ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP).

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: You can have both. If new symmetrical joint swelling develops, see your GP within 6 weeks — early RA treatment is time-critical.

/guides/arthritis-vs-fibromyalgia.title: Arthritis vs Fibromyalgia
/guides/arthritis-vs-fibromyalgia.description: Arthritis is joint disease — pain, stiffness and often swelling in specific joints, visible on examination or imaging. Fibromyalgia is a widespread pain-proc...
/guides/arthritis-vs-fibromyalgia.question: How do I know if it's arthritis or fibromyalgia?
/guides/arthritis-vs-fibromyalgia.answer: Arthritis is joint disease — pain, stiffness and often swelling in specific joints, visible on examination or imaging. Fibromyalgia is a widespread pain-processing condition — pain and tenderness spread across the body, plus fatigue, poor sleep and 'fibro fog', with normal joint examination and imaging. It's common to have both. Diagnosis of fibromyalgia is clinical, based on ACR criteria.

faqs.q: When would you pick Arthritis?
faqs.a: Localised joint pain; visible swelling; imaging changes; morning stiffness in specific joints.

faqs.q: When would you pick Fibromyalgia?
faqs.a: Widespread body pain; tenderness on touch; fatigue; sleep issues; 'fibro fog'.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Both respond to graded exercise, sleep hygiene and CBT — different medications from your GP.

/guides/tendonitis-vs-arthritis.title: Tendonitis vs Arthritis
/guides/tendonitis-vs-arthritis.description: Tendonitis is inflammation of the tendon attaching muscle to bone — pain is usually on movement, tender to touch over the tendon, and improves with rest and ...
/guides/tendonitis-vs-arthritis.question: Is my joint pain tendonitis or arthritis?
/guides/tendonitis-vs-arthritis.answer: Tendonitis is inflammation of the tendon attaching muscle to bone — pain is usually on movement, tender to touch over the tendon, and improves with rest and gradual loading. Arthritis pain comes from inside the joint itself — worse with weight-bearing (OA) or with inflammation regardless of use (RA), often stiff first thing. Physiotherapy assessment is the fastest way to tell them apart.

faqs.q: When would you pick Tendonitis?
faqs.a: Recent onset; specific tender point; movement-related; often after over-use.

faqs.q: When would you pick Arthritis?
faqs.a: Gradual onset; joint stiffness; swelling inside the joint; often symmetrical (RA).

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: The two often coexist — arthritis around a joint can trigger tendonitis nearby.

/guides/bursitis-vs-arthritis.title: Bursitis vs Arthritis
/guides/bursitis-vs-arthritis.description: Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa — a fluid sac that cushions between joints and tendons, most often in the shoulder, hip or knee. Pain is usually localise...
/guides/bursitis-vs-arthritis.question: Is it bursitis or arthritis?
/guides/bursitis-vs-arthritis.answer: Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa — a fluid sac that cushions between joints and tendons, most often in the shoulder, hip or knee. Pain is usually localised, worse with pressure and movement in a specific direction. Arthritis pain is inside the joint. Bursitis often responds well to rest, ice, NSAIDs and a targeted injection; arthritis is a longer-term condition needing a treatment plan.

faqs.q: When would you pick Bursitis?
faqs.a: Sudden onset; tender to touch over a specific spot; pain when lying on that side.

faqs.q: When would you pick Arthritis?
faqs.a: Gradual onset; joint stiffness; imaging changes; pattern typical of OA or RA.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Repeated bursitis in the same joint can suggest underlying arthritis — worth investigating.

/guides/sciatica-vs-hip-arthritis.title: Sciatica vs Hip Arthritis
/guides/sciatica-vs-hip-arthritis.description: Sciatica is nerve pain radiating from the lower back down the leg, often with tingling, numbness or shooting pain past the knee. Hip arthritis pain is felt i...
/guides/sciatica-vs-hip-arthritis.question: Is my pain sciatica or hip arthritis?
/guides/sciatica-vs-hip-arthritis.answer: Sciatica is nerve pain radiating from the lower back down the leg, often with tingling, numbness or shooting pain past the knee. Hip arthritis pain is felt in the groin, buttock or thigh, and rarely goes past the knee. Both can hurt when sitting for a long time, but a physiotherapy or GP examination can quickly distinguish them.

faqs.q: When would you pick Sciatica?
faqs.a: Shooting pain past the knee; tingling/numbness; often triggered by a specific movement.

faqs.q: When would you pick Hip osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: Groin/buttock pain; stiffness putting on socks; hip movement painful on examination.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: You can have both — spinal and hip degeneration often coexist over 60.

/guides/physio-self-referral-vs-gp-refer.title: Physio Self-Referral vs GP Referral
/guides/physio-self-referral-vs-gp-refer.description: In most parts of England, Wales and Scotland you can now self-refer directly to NHS MSK physiotherapy — no GP appointment needed. This is faster and doesn't ...
/guides/physio-self-referral-vs-gp-refer.question: Do I need to see my GP before physiotherapy?
/guides/physio-self-referral-vs-gp-refer.answer: In most parts of England, Wales and Scotland you can now self-refer directly to NHS MSK physiotherapy — no GP appointment needed. This is faster and doesn't cost your GP an appointment slot. Search 'NHS physiotherapy self referral [your area]' — the online form takes ~10 minutes. If self-referral isn't available in your area, or you have red-flag symptoms (numbness, loss of bladder control, unexplained weight loss), see your GP first.

faqs.q: When would you pick Self-refer to NHS physio?
faqs.a: MSK pain (joint, muscle, back); no red-flag symptoms; you know self-referral works in your area.

faqs.q: When would you pick See GP first?
faqs.a: Red-flag symptoms; suspected inflammatory arthritis (needs blood tests/rheumatology); self-referral not available locally.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Waiting times for self-referral are usually similar to GP-referred routes — the benefit is speed of getting the referral in.

/guides/pip-vs-attendance-allowance.title: PIP vs Attendance Allowance for Arthritis
/guides/pip-vs-attendance-allowance.description: Personal Independence Payment (PIP) is for people aged 16 to State Pension age with a long-term condition affecting daily life or mobility. Attendance Allowa...
/guides/pip-vs-attendance-allowance.breadcrumb: PIP vs Attendance Allowance for Arthritis
/guides/pip-vs-attendance-allowance.question: Should I claim PIP or Attendance Allowance?
/guides/pip-vs-attendance-allowance.answer: Personal Independence Payment (PIP) is for people aged 16 to State Pension age with a long-term condition affecting daily life or mobility. Attendance Allowance is for people over State Pension age who need help with personal care because of a disability or illness. You can't claim both. If you're already claiming PIP when you reach State Pension age, you can keep it.

faqs.q: When would you pick PIP (Personal Independence Payment)?
faqs.a: Aged 16 to State Pension age; long-term condition; help needed with daily life or getting around.

faqs.q: When would you pick Attendance Allowance?
faqs.a: Over State Pension age; need help with personal care because of arthritis or other illness.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Both are non-means-tested and don't affect other benefits. Citizens Advice offers free application help.

/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking.title: Blue Badge vs Disability Parking Concessions
/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking.description: A Blue Badge is a UK-wide scheme giving parking concessions to people with severe mobility problems, including those with arthritis that significantly affect...
/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking.breadcrumb: Blue Badge vs Disability Parking Concessions
/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking.question: Do I qualify for a Blue Badge with arthritis?
/guides/blue-badge-vs-disability-parking.answer: A Blue Badge is a UK-wide scheme giving parking concessions to people with severe mobility problems, including those with arthritis that significantly affects walking. You automatically qualify if you get the higher-rate mobility component of PIP or DLA; otherwise you can apply on 'discretionary' grounds by describing how far and comfortably you can walk. Local council disability parking bays and hospital blue-zone bays are separate schemes.

faqs.q: When would you pick Blue Badge?
faqs.a: Severe walking difficulty; qualifies for higher-rate PIP mobility; nationwide use.

faqs.q: When would you pick Local disabled parking?
faqs.a: Occasional need close to home/work; council-specific bays; supplements a Blue Badge.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Renewal is every 3 years and the fee is £10 in England, free in Wales and Scotland.

/guides/wet-vs-dry-heat-therapy.title: Wet Heat vs Dry Heat for Arthritis
/guides/wet-vs-dry-heat-therapy.description: Wet heat (warm bath, hot shower, hydrotherapy) penetrates deeper and treats larger areas — best for widespread stiffness and multiple joints. Dry heat (heat ...
/guides/wet-vs-dry-heat-therapy.breadcrumb: Wet Heat vs Dry Heat for Arthritis
/guides/wet-vs-dry-heat-therapy.question: Is a warm bath or a heat pad better for arthritis?
/guides/wet-vs-dry-heat-therapy.answer: Wet heat (warm bath, hot shower, hydrotherapy) penetrates deeper and treats larger areas — best for widespread stiffness and multiple joints. Dry heat (heat pad, wheat bag, electric blanket) is easier and safer to use targeted at one joint. Both work; combine them (warm shower in the morning, heat pad on the sore knee in the evening).

faqs.q: When would you pick Wet heat?
faqs.a: Widespread stiffness; multiple joints; RA flares; feels good on your body.

faqs.q: When would you pick Dry heat?
faqs.a: One specific joint; easy daytime use; safe for people at risk of falls in the bath.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Never bathe in water hotter than 40°C; test with an elbow first, especially if you have circulation issues or diabetes.

/guides/resistance-bands-vs-weights.title: Resistance Bands vs Weights for Arthritis
/guides/resistance-bands-vs-weights.description: Resistance bands are gentler on joints, easier to modify, portable and cheap — the standard NHS/physio recommendation for starting strength work with arthrit...
/guides/resistance-bands-vs-weights.breadcrumb: Resistance Bands vs Weights for Arthritis
/guides/resistance-bands-vs-weights.question: Should I use resistance bands or weights for arthritis?
/guides/resistance-bands-vs-weights.answer: Resistance bands are gentler on joints, easier to modify, portable and cheap — the standard NHS/physio recommendation for starting strength work with arthritis. Free weights and machines allow heavier loading and are excellent as you progress. Both build the muscle strength that protects joints; start with bands and add weights as confidence grows.

faqs.q: When would you pick Resistance bands?
faqs.a: Beginners; hand arthritis; anyone worried about pain; home use.

faqs.q: When would you pick Free weights / machines?
faqs.a: Progressing after a few months of bands; wanting heavier resistance; supervised gym setting.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: See a physiotherapist for a personalised programme — the wrong exercises can flare arthritis.

/guides/standing-desk-vs-sitting-desk.title: Standing Desk vs Sitting Desk for Arthritis
/guides/standing-desk-vs-sitting-desk.description: Sit-stand desks (adjustable height) are much better than pure standing or pure sitting for anyone with arthritis. Prolonged sitting stiffens joints; prolonge...
/guides/standing-desk-vs-sitting-desk.breadcrumb: Standing Desk vs Sitting Desk for Arthritis
/guides/standing-desk-vs-sitting-desk.question: Is a standing desk better for arthritis?
/guides/standing-desk-vs-sitting-desk.answer: Sit-stand desks (adjustable height) are much better than pure standing or pure sitting for anyone with arthritis. Prolonged sitting stiffens joints; prolonged standing loads knees and hips. The evidence is that alternating every 30-60 minutes reduces back and joint pain more than either extreme. Add a good chair, foot rest, and a monitor at eye level.

faqs.q: When would you pick Sit-stand desk (alternating)?
faqs.a: Anyone with hip, knee or back arthritis; office workers with stiffness; hybrid workers.

faqs.q: When would you pick Fixed sitting desk?
faqs.a: You have severe standing pain and can't tolerate it even briefly.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Standing desks aren't a magic fix — a well-set-up sitting desk with regular movement breaks is usually better than a poorly set-up standing one.

/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.title: Mediterranean Diet vs Anti-Inflammatory Diet
/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.description: The Mediterranean diet is the best-studied anti-inflammatory eating pattern — high in olive oil, oily fish, vegetables, wholegrains, nuts and legumes, low in...
/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.question: Is the Mediterranean diet the same as an anti-inflammatory diet?
/guides/mediterranean-diet-vs-anti-infla.answer: The Mediterranean diet is the best-studied anti-inflammatory eating pattern — high in olive oil, oily fish, vegetables, wholegrains, nuts and legumes, low in red meat and processed food. 'Anti-inflammatory diet' is a broader marketing term that overlaps heavily. For UK arthritis patients, the practical answer is the same: follow a Mediterranean-style pattern using British supermarket ingredients.

faqs.q: When would you pick Mediterranean diet?
faqs.a: Best evidence base; sustainable long-term; supports heart, brain, joint and mental health.

faqs.q: When would you pick General 'anti-inflammatory' diet?
faqs.a: You already follow one; you're looking for specific elimination or supplement guidance.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Don't cut foods without medical advice — restrictive diets can cause nutritional gaps, especially in older adults.

/guides/magnesium-vs-vitamin-d.title: Magnesium vs Vitamin D for Arthritis
/guides/magnesium-vs-vitamin-d.description: The NHS recommends most UK adults take 10 micrograms of vitamin D daily from October to March because sunlight is inadequate — this is especially important f...
/guides/magnesium-vs-vitamin-d.breadcrumb: Magnesium vs Vitamin D for Arthritis
/guides/magnesium-vs-vitamin-d.question: Should I take magnesium or vitamin D for arthritis?
/guides/magnesium-vs-vitamin-d.answer: The NHS recommends most UK adults take 10 micrograms of vitamin D daily from October to March because sunlight is inadequate — this is especially important for bone health with arthritis. Magnesium supplementation is only usually needed if you're deficient (rare unless you have specific conditions). If in doubt, get your GP to check both with a blood test.

faqs.q: When would you pick Vitamin D (10 mcg daily)?
faqs.a: All UK adults in winter; anyone at risk of osteoporosis; steroid users.

faqs.q: When would you pick Magnesium?
faqs.a: Only if a blood test shows you're deficient, or on GP advice.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: High-dose vitamin D (>100 mcg/day) can be harmful. Stick to the NHS-recommended dose unless a doctor advises otherwise.

/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi.title: Chair Yoga vs Tai Chi for Arthritis
/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi.description: Both are excellent low-impact options with strong evidence in older adults. Chair yoga is more accessible if standing is painful or unsafe — you can do it fr...
/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi.breadcrumb: Chair Yoga vs Tai Chi for Arthritis
/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi.question: Should I try chair yoga or tai chi for arthritis?
/guides/chair-yoga-vs-tai-chi.answer: Both are excellent low-impact options with strong evidence in older adults. Chair yoga is more accessible if standing is painful or unsafe — you can do it from a stable chair with no equipment. Tai chi requires standing balance but has the strongest evidence for reducing falls in older adults with arthritis (roughly 30% fewer falls in NHS-endorsed trials).

faqs.q: When would you pick Chair yoga?
faqs.a: Severe knee/hip pain; poor balance; can't stand for long; recovering from surgery.

faqs.q: When would you pick Tai chi?
faqs.a: You can stand safely; want falls-prevention benefit; enjoy a group class.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Look for instructors trained in adaptations for arthritis — search 'arthritis-adapted' or 'senior-focused'.

/guides/meditation-vs-cbt-arthritis-pain.title: Meditation vs CBT for Arthritis Pain
/guides/meditation-vs-cbt-arthritis-pain.description: Both are recommended by NICE for chronic pain and help substantially. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) has the stronger evidence base for reducing pain in...
/guides/meditation-vs-cbt-arthritis-pain.breadcrumb: Meditation vs CBT for Arthritis Pain
/guides/meditation-vs-cbt-arthritis-pain.question: Does meditation or CBT work better for chronic arthritis pain?
/guides/meditation-vs-cbt-arthritis-pain.answer: Both are recommended by NICE for chronic pain and help substantially. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) has the stronger evidence base for reducing pain interference in daily life and low mood. Mindfulness-based meditation (MBSR/MBCT) also reduces pain intensity and improves sleep. For UK residents, NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) offers both free of charge — self-refer online.

faqs.q: When would you pick CBT for chronic pain?
faqs.a: Pain is affecting mood, work or sleep; you want structured, goal-based help.

faqs.q: When would you pick Mindfulness meditation?
faqs.a: You want a self-guided daily practice; you've tried CBT already.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Free access via NHS Talking Therapies (self-refer) or Every Mind Matters. Private CBT £60-100/session.

/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthrit.title: Cold Plunge vs Warm Bath for Arthritis
/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthrit.description: For arthritis, a warm bath is safer and better-evidenced than cold plunging. Warm water eases stiffness, relaxes muscle tension around joints, and supports g...
/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthrit.breadcrumb: Cold Plunge vs Warm Bath for Arthritis
/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthrit.question: Is a cold plunge or warm bath better for arthritis?
/guides/cold-plunge-vs-warm-bath-arthrit.answer: For arthritis, a warm bath is safer and better-evidenced than cold plunging. Warm water eases stiffness, relaxes muscle tension around joints, and supports gentle movement. Cold plunging is trending but the evidence in arthritis is very limited, and it can trigger flare-ups in inflammatory conditions, worsen Raynaud's, and be dangerous for people with heart conditions.

faqs.q: When would you pick Warm bath / hydrotherapy pool (33-36°C)?
faqs.a: Stiffness; RA/OA; muscle tension; before or after exercise.

faqs.q: When would you pick Cold plunge (<15°C)?
faqs.a: Not recommended for most arthritis. If you want cold exposure, use targeted ice packs on inflamed joints only.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Never cold plunge if you have heart disease, high blood pressure, Raynaud's, or you're pregnant, without medical advice.

/guides/dog-arthritis-supplements-vs-pre.title: Joint Supplements vs Prescription Meds for Dogs with Arthritis
/guides/dog-arthritis-supplements-vs-pre.description: For UK dogs with arthritis, veterinary evidence supports starting with a comprehensive plan: weight management, joint-friendly exercise, and a quality supple...
/guides/dog-arthritis-supplements-vs-pre.breadcrumb: Joint Supplements vs Prescription Meds for Dogs with Arthritis
/guides/dog-arthritis-supplements-vs-pre.question: Should I give my dog joint supplements or vet-prescribed medication?
/guides/dog-arthritis-supplements-vs-pre.answer: For UK dogs with arthritis, veterinary evidence supports starting with a comprehensive plan: weight management, joint-friendly exercise, and a quality supplement (glucosamine, chondroitin, green-lipped mussel, omega-3). Prescription options like NSAIDs (meloxicam, carprofen) or Librela (an antibody injection) are added when supplements alone aren't enough — always under vet supervision, not self-prescribed.

faqs.q: When would you pick Joint supplements (Yumove, glucosamine)?
faqs.a: Mild-to-moderate signs; part of a long-term plan; alongside weight and exercise.

faqs.q: When would you pick Vet-prescribed medication (NSAIDs, Librela)?
faqs.a: Persistent limping; night pain; reduced quality of life; supplements alone aren't enough.

faqs.q: What should I be careful about?
faqs.a: Never give a dog human painkillers — paracetamol and ibuprofen can be fatal. Always consult your vet.

/glossary/dmard.title: DMARD: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/dmard.description: Disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug — slows joint damage in inflammatory arthritis.
/glossary/dmard.question: What is dmard?
/glossary/dmard.answer: DMARD: DMARDs are drugs that slow the underlying disease process in inflammatory arthritis (RA, PsA, JIA). Conventional DMARDs include methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine and leflunomide. Starting a DMARD within 3 months of RA symptoms significantly reduces long-term joint damage. All require regular blood monitoring.

/glossary/biologic.title: Biologic: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/biologic.description: Injected/infused drug targeting a specific part of the immune system.
/glossary/biologic.question: What is biologic?
/glossary/biologic.answer: Biologic: Biologics are targeted immune-system drugs used when conventional DMARDs alone don't control inflammatory arthritis. UK NICE approves them based on disease activity scores. Examples: adalimumab, etanercept, tocilizumab, rituximab. They increase infection risk so vaccinations and screening are essential.

/glossary/nsaid.title: NSAID: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/nsaid.question: What is nsaid?
/glossary/nsaid.answer: NSAID: NSAIDs reduce pain and inflammation but carry stomach, kidney and heart risk with sustained use. NICE recommends topical NSAIDs first for hand/knee OA. Take with food; check with pharmacist if over 65, taking blood thinners, or with kidney/heart conditions.

/glossary/corticosteroid.title: Corticosteroid: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/corticosteroid.description: Anti-inflammatory drug given as tablet, injection or infusion.
/glossary/corticosteroid.question: What is corticosteroid?
/glossary/corticosteroid.answer: Corticosteroid: Corticosteroids (prednisolone, methylprednisolone, hydrocortisone) rapidly reduce inflammation but have long-term side effects: weight gain, high blood sugar, bone thinning, mood changes. Used short-term for flares or as targeted joint injections.

/glossary/synovium.title: Synovium: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/synovium.description: Thin lining of a joint that produces lubricating fluid.
/glossary/synovium.question: What is synovium?
/glossary/synovium.answer: Synovium: The synovium is the thin membrane lining the inside of a joint capsule. It produces synovial fluid, which lubricates and nourishes cartilage. In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the synovium, causing swelling, warmth and long-term joint damage.

/glossary/cartilage.title: Cartilage: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/cartilage.description: Smooth tissue covering the ends of bones in a joint.
/glossary/cartilage.question: What is cartilage?
/glossary/cartilage.answer: Cartilage: Cartilage is the smooth, tough connective tissue capping the ends of bones where they meet in joints. It cushions impact and allows friction-free movement. In osteoarthritis, cartilage gradually thins and roughens; it has no direct blood supply so heals slowly.

/glossary/hla-b27.title: HLA-B27: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/hla-b27.description: A gene marker linked to inflammatory spinal arthritis.
/glossary/hla-b27.question: What is hla-b27?
/glossary/hla-b27.answer: HLA-B27: HLA-B27 is a genetic marker present in ~90% of people with ankylosing spondylitis, but also in ~8% of the general UK population without disease. A positive test alone doesn't diagnose disease — clinical assessment and imaging are essential.

/glossary/rheumatoid-factor.title: Rheumatoid factor: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/rheumatoid-factor.description: A blood antibody found in most people with rheumatoid arthritis.
/glossary/rheumatoid-factor.question: What is rheumatoid factor?
/glossary/rheumatoid-factor.answer: Rheumatoid factor: Rheumatoid factor (RF) is an antibody detected in roughly 70-80% of people with rheumatoid arthritis. Can also be positive in other conditions (Sjögren's, chronic infections) and in ~5% of healthy older adults, so it's diagnostic only with symptoms.

/glossary/anti-ccp.title: Anti-CCP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/anti-ccp.description: A more specific blood test for rheumatoid arthritis.
/glossary/anti-ccp.question: What is anti-ccp?
/glossary/anti-ccp.answer: Anti-CCP: Anti-CCP (anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide) antibodies are more specific than rheumatoid factor for diagnosing RA. Positive anti-CCP predicts more aggressive disease and helps rheumatologists decide on early aggressive treatment.

/glossary/esr.title: ESR: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/esr.description: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate — blood test for inflammation.
/glossary/esr.question: What is esr?
/glossary/esr.answer: ESR: ESR measures how quickly red blood cells settle in a tube, indirectly indicating inflammation. Elevated in inflammatory arthritis, infections, and other conditions. Used alongside CRP to monitor disease activity, not for diagnosis alone.

/glossary/crp.title: CRP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/crp.description: C-reactive protein — a faster blood marker of inflammation.
/glossary/crp.question: What is crp?
/glossary/crp.answer: CRP: CRP is a protein made by the liver in response to inflammation. Rises faster than ESR (hours vs days) and drops more quickly when inflammation resolves. Used to monitor flares and treatment response in inflammatory arthritis.

/glossary/joint-effusion.title: Joint effusion: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/joint-effusion.description: Fluid build-up inside a joint causing swelling.
/glossary/joint-effusion.question: What is joint effusion?
/glossary/joint-effusion.answer: Joint effusion: A joint effusion is abnormal accumulation of fluid inside the joint capsule, causing visible swelling, tightness and reduced movement. Common in OA, RA, gout, trauma or infection. May be drained (aspirated) to relieve symptoms and analyse the cause.

/glossary/crepitus.title: Crepitus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/crepitus.description: The grating or crackling sound in a moving joint.
/glossary/crepitus.question: What is crepitus?
/glossary/crepitus.answer: Crepitus: Crepitus is the audible or palpable grating, crackling or clicking felt when a joint moves. Common in OA and often harmless in isolation — many people over 40 have crepitus without pain. Concerning if painful or new.

/glossary/flare.title: Flare: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/flare.description: A period when arthritis symptoms suddenly worsen.
/glossary/flare.question: What is flare?
/glossary/flare.answer: Flare: A flare is a sudden or gradual worsening of arthritis symptoms — more pain, stiffness, swelling and fatigue — lasting days to weeks. Common triggers: stress, illness, over-exertion, weather changes, missed medication. Have a written flare plan agreed with your rheumatology team.

/glossary/remission.title: Remission: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/remission.description: When arthritis symptoms are absent or minimal.
/glossary/remission.question: What is remission?
/glossary/remission.answer: Remission: Remission means very low or absent disease activity, measured by symptoms and blood markers. In RA, drug-induced remission is now a realistic goal with early DMARDs. Medication is usually continued even during remission to prevent flares.

/glossary/seronegative.title: Seronegative: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/seronegative.description: Arthritis with negative blood tests for RA antibodies.
/glossary/seronegative.question: What is seronegative?
/glossary/seronegative.answer: Seronegative: Seronegative arthritis means inflammatory joint disease without positive RF or anti-CCP tests. Includes AS, PsA, reactive arthritis. Diagnosis relies on clinical picture and imaging; management is similar to seropositive disease.

/glossary/enthesitis.title: Enthesitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/enthesitis.description: Inflammation where a tendon or ligament joins bone.
/glossary/enthesitis.question: What is enthesitis?
/glossary/enthesitis.answer: Enthesitis: Enthesitis is inflammation at the entheses — where tendons or ligaments attach to bone. Characteristic of spondyloarthropathies (AS, PsA) and often the first symptom (e.g. Achilles tendon pain, plantar fasciitis).

/glossary/dactylitis.title: Dactylitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/dactylitis.description: Sausage-like swelling of an entire finger or toe.
/glossary/dactylitis.question: What is dactylitis?
/glossary/dactylitis.answer: Dactylitis: Dactylitis is swelling of a whole digit ('sausage finger' or 'sausage toe') from combined joint and tendon inflammation. Highly characteristic of psoriatic and reactive arthritis. Requires rheumatology assessment.

/glossary/morning-stiffness.title: Morning stiffness: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/morning-stiffness.description: Joint stiffness first thing after waking.
/glossary/morning-stiffness.question: What is morning stiffness?
/glossary/morning-stiffness.answer: Morning stiffness: Morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes is typical of osteoarthritis. Stiffness over an hour, especially symmetrical, points to inflammatory arthritis like RA and needs urgent GP review. Duration is a key diagnostic clue.

/glossary/osteophyte.title: Osteophyte: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/osteophyte.description: A bony spur that grows near an arthritic joint.
/glossary/osteophyte.question: What is osteophyte?
/glossary/osteophyte.answer: Osteophyte: Osteophytes ('bone spurs') are bony outgrowths at the edges of joints damaged by osteoarthritis. Show clearly on X-rays. They can restrict movement and, in the spine, sometimes press on nerves — but many are painless.

/glossary/subchondral.title: Subchondral bone: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/subchondral.description: The bone just underneath the joint cartilage.
/glossary/subchondral.question: What is subchondral bone?
/glossary/subchondral.answer: Subchondral bone: Subchondral bone lies immediately beneath the joint cartilage. In OA, it thickens ('sclerosis'), may develop small holes ('cysts') and gets damaged as cartilage thins. Changes are visible on X-ray and are diagnostic.

/glossary/pannus.title: Pannus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/pannus.description: Inflamed tissue that invades and damages joints in RA.
/glossary/pannus.question: What is pannus?
/glossary/pannus.answer: Pannus: Pannus is abnormal granulation tissue that grows in RA-affected joints, releasing enzymes that erode cartilage and bone. Early effective DMARD treatment prevents pannus formation and the resulting joint damage.

/glossary/ankylosis.title: Ankylosis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/ankylosis.description: Fusion of bones in a joint.
/glossary/ankylosis.question: What is ankylosis?
/glossary/ankylosis.answer: Ankylosis: Ankylosis is stiffening or fusion of a joint, either bony (in ankylosing spondylitis) or fibrous. Untreated inflammation and immobility promote it. Prevention through medication and exercise is far more effective than reversal.

/glossary/uric-acid.title: Uric acid: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/uric-acid.description: A waste product that forms crystals in gout.
/glossary/uric-acid.question: What is uric acid?
/glossary/uric-acid.answer: Uric acid: Uric acid is a natural waste product of purine breakdown. High blood levels ('hyperuricaemia') can crystallise in joints, causing gout attacks. Managed by lowering intake (alcohol, offal, seafood) and, when attacks recur, urate-lowering drugs (allopurinol).

/glossary/tophi.title: Tophi: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/tophi.description: Chalky uric acid deposits under the skin in chronic gout.
/glossary/tophi.question: What is tophi?
/glossary/tophi.answer: Tophi: Tophi are visible or palpable lumps of urate crystals in the skin, ears, tendons or joints in long-standing gout. They cause deformity and joint damage. Their presence means urate-lowering therapy is essential.

/glossary/physiotherapy-triage.title: Physiotherapy triage: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/physiotherapy-triage.description: Assessment to decide the right care pathway.
/glossary/physiotherapy-triage.question: What is physiotherapy triage?
/glossary/physiotherapy-triage.answer: Physiotherapy triage: Physiotherapy triage is an initial assessment (often by a First Contact Practitioner in general practice) to sort MSK problems into: self-management, physio treatment, imaging, or specialist referral. Reduces GP burden and speeds care.

/glossary/musculoskeletal.title: Musculoskeletal (MSK): Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/musculoskeletal.description: Related to muscles, bones, joints, tendons and ligaments.
/glossary/musculoskeletal.question: What is musculoskeletal (msk)?
/glossary/musculoskeletal.answer: Musculoskeletal (MSK): 'Musculoskeletal' means anything involving muscles, bones, joints, tendons or ligaments. MSK conditions are the leading cause of work absence and disability in the UK, affecting around 20 million people. Most GP visits for back pain, joint pain and sports injuries are MSK.

/glossary/proprioception.title: Proprioception: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/proprioception.description: The body's sense of where its joints are.
/glossary/proprioception.question: What is proprioception?
/glossary/proprioception.answer: Proprioception: Proprioception is your brain's awareness of joint position without looking. Arthritis and joint injury impair proprioception, worsening balance and falls risk. Specific balance and coordination exercises restore it.

/glossary/range-of-motion.title: Range of motion (ROM): Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/range-of-motion.description: How far a joint can move in each direction.
/glossary/range-of-motion.question: What is range of motion (rom)?
/glossary/range-of-motion.answer: Range of motion (ROM): ROM is the measurable extent of movement at a joint — flexion, extension, rotation. Physiotherapists compare your ROM to normal ranges and track improvement. Regular gentle movement preserves ROM even in painful joints.

/glossary/passive-vs-active-movement.title: Passive vs active movement: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/passive-vs-active-movement.description: Someone moves your joint for you vs you move it yourself.
/glossary/passive-vs-active-movement.question: What is passive vs active movement?
/glossary/passive-vs-active-movement.answer: Passive vs active movement: Passive movement is when a therapist moves your joint through its range without you contracting muscles. Active movement is when you do it yourself. Both are used in arthritis rehabilitation — passive keeps joints supple; active builds strength.

/glossary/hydrotherapy.title: Hydrotherapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/hydrotherapy.description: Exercise in a heated pool for pain relief and mobility.
/glossary/hydrotherapy.question: What is hydrotherapy?
/glossary/hydrotherapy.answer: Hydrotherapy: Hydrotherapy is supervised exercise in a warm pool (33-36°C). Water reduces joint load and warmth eases pain, allowing movement that isn't possible on land. NHS access varies; some rheumatology units offer courses.

/glossary/occupational-therapy.title: Occupational therapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/occupational-therapy.description: Practical help adapting daily activities to your condition.
/glossary/occupational-therapy.question: What is occupational therapy?
/glossary/occupational-therapy.answer: Occupational therapy: Occupational therapists (OTs) help with practical daily activities — dressing, cooking, work, hobbies — using adapted techniques, aids and equipment. NHS OTs assess your home and provide equipment such as grab rails free of charge.

/glossary/nice.title: NICE: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/nice.description: The UK body that publishes health guidance.
/glossary/nice.question: What is nice?
/glossary/nice.answer: NICE: The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) develops evidence-based guidelines for the NHS in England (and adopted by Wales/NI). Key arthritis guidelines: NG226 (OA), NG100 (RA), CG79 (RA in adults). Your care should broadly follow NICE guidance.

/glossary/pip.title: PIP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/pip.description: Personal Independence Payment, a UK disability benefit.
/glossary/pip.question: What is pip?
/glossary/pip.answer: PIP: PIP is a non-means-tested benefit for people aged 16 to State Pension age with a long-term condition affecting daily life or mobility. Assessed on functional impact, not diagnosis. Arthritis frequently qualifies; Citizens Advice offers free application help.

/glossary/attendance-allowance.title: Attendance Allowance: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/attendance-allowance.description: A UK benefit for people over State Pension age with a care need.
/glossary/attendance-allowance.question: What is attendance allowance?
/glossary/attendance-allowance.answer: Attendance Allowance: Attendance Allowance is a non-means-tested benefit for people over State Pension age who need help with personal care because of illness or disability. £68.10-£101.75/week (2025 rates). Doesn't require an assessment of ability to walk.

/glossary/blue-badge.title: Blue Badge: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
