/glossary/blue-badge.description: UK parking concession for people with severe mobility problems.
/glossary/blue-badge.question: What is blue badge?
/glossary/blue-badge.answer: Blue Badge: The Blue Badge is a UK-wide parking scheme giving concessions to people with severe walking difficulty. Automatic eligibility with higher-rate PIP mobility; discretionary applications also possible. Fee £10 in England, free in Wales/Scotland.

/glossary/gp-referral.title: GP referral: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/gp-referral.description: When your GP refers you to a specialist.
/glossary/gp-referral.question: What is gp referral?
/glossary/gp-referral.answer: GP referral: GP referral is the standard NHS route to see a specialist (rheumatologist, orthopaedic surgeon). For MSK physio, many areas now allow self-referral without GP. Waiting times for rheumatology first appointment: 4-30 weeks depending on area.

/glossary/self-referral.title: Self-referral: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/self-referral.description: Booking NHS physiotherapy without a GP appointment.
/glossary/self-referral.question: What is self-referral?
/glossary/self-referral.answer: Self-referral: Self-referral means going directly to an NHS service without a GP letter. Common for MSK physiotherapy, IAPT/Talking Therapies and sexual health. Search 'NHS [service] self referral [your area]'. Saves both your and your GP's time.

/glossary/triple-therapy.title: Triple therapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/triple-therapy.description: Combining three DMARDs in rheumatoid arthritis.
/glossary/triple-therapy.question: What is triple therapy?
/glossary/triple-therapy.answer: Triple therapy: Triple therapy typically means methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine, an evidence-based combination for people with RA whose disease isn't controlled on methotrexate alone. Cheaper alternative to biologics with comparable outcomes for some patients.

/glossary/methotrexate.title: Methotrexate: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/methotrexate.question: What is methotrexate?
/glossary/methotrexate.answer: Methotrexate: Methotrexate is the anchor drug for rheumatoid arthritis and many inflammatory conditions, usually taken once weekly with folic acid on other days. Requires regular blood tests. Common side effects (nausea, tiredness) often improve after a few months.

/glossary/sulfasalazine.title: Sulfasalazine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/sulfasalazine.question: What is sulfasalazine?
/glossary/sulfasalazine.answer: Sulfasalazine: Sulfasalazine is a well-established DMARD used for RA and some spondyloarthropathies. Taken as tablets. Common in the UK because it's affordable and safe in pregnancy (unlike methotrexate). Can cause harmless orange discolouration of urine and skin.

/glossary/hydroxychloroquine.title: Hydroxychloroquine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/hydroxychloroquine.description: A DMARD often used in mild RA and lupus.
/glossary/hydroxychloroquine.question: What is hydroxychloroquine?
/glossary/hydroxychloroquine.answer: Hydroxychloroquine: Hydroxychloroquine is a well-tolerated DMARD used in lupus, mild RA and combination therapy. Requires annual eye checks because of a small long-term retinal risk. Safe in pregnancy.

/glossary/leflunomide.title: Leflunomide: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/leflunomide.description: A conventional DMARD used in RA and PsA.
/glossary/leflunomide.question: What is leflunomide?
/glossary/leflunomide.answer: Leflunomide: Leflunomide is an oral DMARD for RA and PsA when methotrexate isn't tolerated or effective. Requires regular blood monitoring and effective contraception in men and women (long half-life).

/glossary/adalimumab.title: Adalimumab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/adalimumab.question: What is adalimumab?
/glossary/adalimumab.answer: Adalimumab: Adalimumab is a biologic that blocks TNF-alpha, used for RA, PsA, AS and other inflammatory conditions. Self-injected every 1-2 weeks. Biosimilars are widely used in the NHS. Screening for TB, hepatitis and current infections is essential before starting.

/glossary/etanercept.title: Etanercept: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/etanercept.question: What is etanercept?
/glossary/etanercept.answer: Etanercept: Etanercept is a TNF-blocking biologic self-injected weekly or twice weekly. Widely used in the UK for RA, PsA, AS and juvenile arthritis. NHS eligibility depends on disease activity scores (DAS28).

/glossary/infliximab.title: Infliximab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/infliximab.description: An anti-TNF biologic given by infusion.
/glossary/infliximab.question: What is infliximab?
/glossary/infliximab.answer: Infliximab: Infliximab is a biologic given by hospital infusion every 6-8 weeks. Used in RA, PsA, AS, Crohn's and other conditions. Requires ongoing hospital appointments but effective and predictable.

/glossary/rituximab.title: Rituximab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/rituximab.question: What is rituximab?
/glossary/rituximab.answer: Rituximab: Rituximab depletes B lymphocytes, given as hospital infusions typically every 6 months. Used when TNF-blockers fail or aren't suitable. Requires screening for hepatitis B and monitoring for infection risk.

/glossary/tocilizumab.title: Tocilizumab: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/tocilizumab.question: What is tocilizumab?
/glossary/tocilizumab.answer: Tocilizumab: Tocilizumab blocks interleukin-6, used in RA, giant cell arteritis and juvenile arthritis. Available as subcutaneous injection or IV infusion. Requires regular blood monitoring.

/glossary/jak-inhibitor.title: JAK inhibitor: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/jak-inhibitor.description: A newer oral targeted arthritis drug.
/glossary/jak-inhibitor.question: What is jak inhibitor?
/glossary/jak-inhibitor.answer: JAK inhibitor: JAK inhibitors (baricitinib, tofacitinib, upadacitinib) are oral drugs that block the JAK-STAT immune signalling pathway. Highly effective in RA and PsA. UK regulators have restricted use in some groups because of cardiovascular and cancer safety data.

/glossary/das28.title: DAS28: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/das28.description: A score for measuring RA disease activity.
/glossary/das28.question: What is das28?
/glossary/das28.answer: DAS28: The Disease Activity Score in 28 joints (DAS28) is used by UK rheumatology to decide treatment escalation. Combines tender joints, swollen joints, ESR/CRP and patient global rating. NICE thresholds determine biologic eligibility.

/glossary/acr-response.title: ACR20/50/70: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/acr-response.question: What is acr20/50/70?
/glossary/acr-response.answer: ACR20/50/70: ACR response criteria (American College of Rheumatology) measure whether patients improve 20%, 50% or 70% in RA trials. Used to compare drugs but rarely quoted directly in NHS clinics.

/glossary/gout-attack.title: Gout attack: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/gout-attack.description: A sudden onset of severe joint pain from urate crystals.
/glossary/gout-attack.question: What is gout attack?
/glossary/gout-attack.answer: Gout attack: A gout attack is sudden severe joint pain, swelling and redness, most often in the big toe. Peaks within 24 hours. Treated with NSAIDs, colchicine or short steroid course. Recurrent attacks need urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol).

/glossary/allopurinol.title: Allopurinol: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/allopurinol.description: The main long-term urate-lowering drug for gout.
/glossary/allopurinol.question: What is allopurinol?
/glossary/allopurinol.answer: Allopurinol: Allopurinol lowers uric acid production and prevents future gout attacks. Started at low dose after the acute attack settles, titrated up over months. Target: uric acid <360 μmol/L, or <300 with tophi.

/glossary/colchicine.title: Colchicine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/colchicine.description: A drug for acute gout attacks.
/glossary/colchicine.question: What is colchicine?
/glossary/colchicine.answer: Colchicine: Colchicine is used for acute gout when NSAIDs aren't suitable. Effective if started early in the attack. Dose reduced from historical high doses because of side effects.

/glossary/uveitis.title: Uveitis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/uveitis.description: Eye inflammation associated with inflammatory arthritis.
/glossary/uveitis.question: What is uveitis?
/glossary/uveitis.answer: Uveitis: Uveitis is inflammation of the eye's uveal tract, causing pain, redness and blurred vision. Strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis and other spondyloarthropathies. Any red painful eye with AS needs same-day ophthalmology assessment.

/glossary/sjogrens.title: Sjögren's syndrome: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/sjogrens.description: An autoimmune condition causing dry eyes and mouth.
/glossary/sjogrens.question: What is sjögren's syndrome?
/glossary/sjogrens.answer: Sjögren's syndrome: Sjögren's syndrome is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks moisture-producing glands, causing dry eyes and mouth. Often coexists with RA and lupus. Managed with tear substitutes, saliva stimulants and immunosuppression when needed.

/glossary/raynauds.title: Raynaud's phenomenon: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/raynauds.description: Fingers/toes turning white and blue in the cold.
/glossary/raynauds.question: What is raynaud's phenomenon?
/glossary/raynauds.answer: Raynaud's phenomenon: Raynaud's is exaggerated cold response — fingers/toes turn white, then blue, then red. Primary Raynaud's is common and benign. Secondary Raynaud's is linked to autoimmune conditions (scleroderma, lupus) and needs specialist review.

/glossary/erythema-migrans.title: Erythema migrans: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/erythema-migrans.description: A characteristic rash of Lyme disease.
/glossary/erythema-migrans.question: What is erythema migrans?
/glossary/erythema-migrans.answer: Erythema migrans: Erythema migrans is the classic expanding 'bulls-eye' rash of early Lyme disease. Antibiotics started early prevent Lyme arthritis and other complications. If you develop joint pain after a tick bite and rash, see your GP promptly.

/glossary/septic-arthritis.title: Septic arthritis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/septic-arthritis.description: Bacterial infection inside a joint — a medical emergency.
/glossary/septic-arthritis.question: What is septic arthritis?
/glossary/septic-arthritis.answer: Septic arthritis: Septic arthritis is bacterial infection of a joint, causing severe pain, swelling, redness, warmth and fever. Requires emergency hospital treatment: joint drainage and IV antibiotics. Delay can destroy the joint within days.

/glossary/rice-protocol.title: RICE: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/rice-protocol.description: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation for joint injuries.
/glossary/rice-protocol.question: What is rice?
/glossary/rice-protocol.answer: RICE: RICE is the classic first-aid protocol for acute joint injury: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Recent evidence (PEACE and LOVE) suggests early gentle movement may be preferable to prolonged rest, but RICE remains a useful starting point.

/glossary/tens.title: TENS: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/tens.description: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation for pain relief.
/glossary/tens.question: What is tens?
/glossary/tens.answer: TENS: TENS units deliver small electrical pulses through skin electrodes to block pain signals. Available from pharmacies for £20-50. Evidence in chronic arthritis pain is modest but many people find them helpful, with no side effects.

/glossary/kinesiology-tape.title: Kinesiology tape: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/kinesiology-tape.description: Elastic tape applied to joints for support.
/glossary/kinesiology-tape.question: What is kinesiology tape?
/glossary/kinesiology-tape.answer: Kinesiology tape: Kinesiology tape is elastic tape applied by physiotherapists to support joints without restricting movement. Evidence for specific pain relief is limited, but many people report benefit as part of a broader rehab plan.

/glossary/orthotics.title: Orthotics: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/orthotics.description: Shoe inserts to redistribute foot and joint load.
/glossary/orthotics.question: What is orthotics?
/glossary/orthotics.answer: Orthotics: Orthotics are custom or off-the-shelf shoe inserts that change how weight passes through the foot, ankle, knee and hip. Helpful for hallux valgus, flat feet, plantar fasciitis and some knee OA. NHS podiatry can prescribe them.

/glossary/acupuncture.title: Acupuncture: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/acupuncture.description: Traditional practice sometimes used for chronic pain.
/glossary/acupuncture.question: What is acupuncture?
/glossary/acupuncture.answer: Acupuncture: Acupuncture uses thin needles at specific body points. NICE no longer recommends it for OA (evidence downgraded), but some people find it helpful for chronic pain as part of a broader plan. Rarely available on NHS for arthritis.

/glossary/cbd.title: CBD: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/cbd.description: Cannabidiol — a cannabis compound used for pain.
/glossary/cbd.question: What is cbd?
/glossary/cbd.answer: CBD: CBD is a non-psychoactive cannabis compound sold in the UK as an over-the-counter supplement. Evidence for arthritis pain relief is preliminary. Legally sold if <0.2% THC. Not the same as prescribed medical cannabis.

/glossary/medical-cannabis.title: Medical cannabis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/medical-cannabis.description: Prescribed cannabis-based products in the UK.
/glossary/medical-cannabis.question: What is medical cannabis?
/glossary/medical-cannabis.answer: Medical cannabis: Medical cannabis has been legal on prescription in the UK since 2018 but is very rarely prescribed for arthritis — usually reserved for specific licensed conditions (severe epilepsy, chemotherapy nausea, MS spasticity).

/glossary/hip-replacement.title: Hip replacement: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/hip-replacement.description: Surgery to replace a worn-out hip joint.
/glossary/hip-replacement.question: What is hip replacement?
/glossary/hip-replacement.answer: Hip replacement: Hip replacement (arthroplasty) replaces the worn-out hip with metal, ceramic and plastic components. Around 100,000 done in the UK yearly. Excellent outcomes for pain and function; modern implants last 20+ years for most.

/glossary/knee-replacement.title: Knee replacement: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/knee-replacement.description: Surgery to replace part or all of a worn knee.
/glossary/knee-replacement.question: What is knee replacement?
/glossary/knee-replacement.answer: Knee replacement: Knee replacement replaces the worn joint surfaces. Total knee replacement is more common than partial. Recovery: hospital stay 1-3 days, walking with aid within weeks, full recovery 6-12 months. Physio before and after is critical.

/glossary/arthrodesis.title: Arthrodesis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/arthrodesis.question: What is arthrodesis?
/glossary/arthrodesis.answer: Arthrodesis: Arthrodesis fuses bones in a joint together, eliminating movement to eliminate pain. Sometimes done in ankles, wrists, spine and small joints when replacement isn't suitable. Trades movement for pain relief.

/glossary/arthroscopy.title: Arthroscopy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/arthroscopy.description: Keyhole surgery to look inside a joint.
/glossary/arthroscopy.question: What is arthroscopy?
/glossary/arthroscopy.answer: Arthroscopy: Arthroscopy is keyhole surgery to diagnose or treat problems inside a joint. Small incisions, thin camera. NICE no longer recommends 'clean-out' arthroscopy for OA — evidence showed no benefit — but it remains useful for specific mechanical problems.

/glossary/osteotomy.title: Osteotomy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/osteotomy.description: Surgery to reshape bone around an arthritic joint.
/glossary/osteotomy.question: What is osteotomy?
/glossary/osteotomy.answer: Osteotomy: Osteotomy cuts and realigns bone to shift load onto a healthier part of the joint. Sometimes used in younger patients with unilateral knee OA to delay replacement. Now less common with modern replacement techniques.

/glossary/meniscus.title: Meniscus: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/meniscus.description: Cartilage disc in the knee that cushions the joint.
/glossary/meniscus.question: What is meniscus?
/glossary/meniscus.answer: Meniscus: The meniscus is a C-shaped cartilage disc in the knee that cushions and stabilises the joint. Age-related tears are common and often symptomless. NICE recommends physiotherapy first for degenerative tears — surgery only for specific mechanical symptoms.

/glossary/labrum.title: Labrum: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/labrum.description: Cartilage rim of the hip or shoulder socket.
/glossary/labrum.question: What is labrum?
/glossary/labrum.answer: Labrum: The labrum is the ring of cartilage around the hip and shoulder sockets, deepening the joint and helping stability. Tears can cause pain and clicking. Some are surgically treated but many respond to physiotherapy.

/glossary/bone-density.title: Bone density (BMD): Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/bone-density.question: What is bone density (bmd)?
/glossary/bone-density.answer: Bone density (BMD): Bone mineral density is measured by DEXA scan, expressed as a T-score. Below -1: osteopenia; below -2.5: osteoporosis. Weight-bearing exercise, calcium, vitamin D and, when needed, bisphosphonates maintain BMD.

/glossary/osteoporosis.title: Osteoporosis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/osteoporosis.description: Low bone density that increases fracture risk.
/glossary/osteoporosis.question: What is osteoporosis?
/glossary/osteoporosis.answer: Osteoporosis: Osteoporosis is silently reduced bone density until a fragility fracture happens. Screening after menopause or long-term steroid use. Managed with lifestyle, calcium, vitamin D and bisphosphonates (alendronic acid) if high risk.

/glossary/frax.title: FRAX score: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/frax.description: A tool that estimates 10-year fracture risk.
/glossary/frax.question: What is frax score?
/glossary/frax.answer: FRAX score: FRAX is an online tool from Sheffield University that estimates your 10-year risk of hip and major fracture based on age, sex, BMI, family and clinical factors. Used by NHS GPs to decide who needs bone-density scanning or treatment.

/glossary/bisphosphonates.title: Bisphosphonates: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/bisphosphonates.question: What is bisphosphonates?
/glossary/bisphosphonates.answer: Bisphosphonates: Bisphosphonates (alendronic acid, risedronate, zoledronic acid) slow bone breakdown and reduce fracture risk in osteoporosis. Weekly tablet or annual infusion. Take on an empty stomach, stay upright 30 min. Rare jaw and thigh bone side effects.

/glossary/sarcopenia.title: Sarcopenia: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/sarcopenia.description: Age-related loss of muscle mass and strength.
/glossary/sarcopenia.question: What is sarcopenia?
/glossary/sarcopenia.answer: Sarcopenia: Sarcopenia is accelerated muscle loss with age, worsened by inactivity and low protein intake. Reversible with resistance training and adequate protein (~1.0-1.2 g/kg/day). Contributes to falls and frailty.

/glossary/frailty.title: Frailty: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/frailty.description: A state of reduced reserve and resilience.
/glossary/frailty.question: What is frailty?
/glossary/frailty.answer: Frailty: Frailty is not the same as ageing — it's reduced physiological reserve making people vulnerable to setbacks. Assessed with tools like the Clinical Frailty Scale. Reversible early: strength training, protein, treating cataracts, medication review.

/glossary/cfs.title: Clinical Frailty Scale: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/cfs.description: A 9-point score used by NHS staff.
/glossary/cfs.question: What is clinical frailty scale?
/glossary/cfs.answer: Clinical Frailty Scale: The Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale rates frailty 1 (very fit) to 9 (terminally ill). Used across the NHS in hospital admissions and community care. Scores 1-3 fit; 4-5 vulnerable; 6+ frail.

/glossary/otago.title: Otago exercise programme: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/otago.description: An NHS-endorsed strength and balance course.
/glossary/otago.question: What is otago exercise programme?
/glossary/otago.answer: Otago exercise programme: The Otago Exercise Programme is a physiotherapy-designed home programme of leg strength and balance exercises. Randomised trial evidence shows ~35% fewer falls in older adults. Available through NHS falls services.

/glossary/falls-risk.title: Falls risk: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/falls-risk.description: Likelihood of falling in the next year.
/glossary/falls-risk.question: What is falls risk?
/glossary/falls-risk.answer: Falls risk: Falls risk in older adults with arthritis is doubled by pain, weakness, poor balance, medications and vision. Assessed via history (previous falls, near-falls), timed-up-and-go test, and medication review. Halveable with structured intervention.

/glossary/ct-scan.title: CT scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/ct-scan.question: What is ct scan?
/glossary/ct-scan.answer: CT scan: CT scans use X-rays to build detailed cross-sectional bone images. Better than plain X-ray for complex fractures and bony detail; poorer than MRI for soft tissue. Uses ionising radiation.

/glossary/mri.title: MRI: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/mri.description: Magnetic resonance imaging — detailed joint imaging.
/glossary/mri.question: What is mri?
/glossary/mri.answer: MRI: MRI uses magnetic fields to image soft tissue and bone marrow in detail. Best for cartilage, ligaments, tendons and early inflammatory changes not visible on X-ray. No radiation. NHS waiting times vary.

/glossary/ultrasound.title: Ultrasound: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/ultrasound.description: Real-time imaging of joints and soft tissue.
/glossary/ultrasound.question: What is ultrasound?
/glossary/ultrasound.answer: Ultrasound: Musculoskeletal ultrasound uses sound waves to image joints, tendons and inflammation in real time. Increasingly used by rheumatologists for early RA detection and injection guidance.

/glossary/bone-scan.title: Bone scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/bone-scan.description: Nuclear medicine test for bone activity.
/glossary/bone-scan.question: What is bone scan?
/glossary/bone-scan.answer: Bone scan: A bone (bone scintigraphy) scan uses a small dose of radioactive tracer taken up by active bone. Used for detecting metastases, hidden fractures, complex regional pain syndrome and bone infections.

/glossary/dexa-scan.title: DEXA scan: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/dexa-scan.description: The standard test for bone density.
/glossary/dexa-scan.question: What is dexa scan?
/glossary/dexa-scan.answer: DEXA scan: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) measures bone mineral density at hip and spine. Standard test for osteoporosis diagnosis. Low radiation dose. NHS available on GP or specialist referral.

/glossary/dass-score.title: DASS: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/dass-score.question: What is dass?
/glossary/dass-score.answer: DASS: DASS is a self-report questionnaire measuring depression, anxiety and stress. Used to identify mental health impact of chronic conditions like arthritis. NHS Talking Therapies uses similar tools to guide treatment.

/glossary/act-therapy.title: ACT: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/act-therapy.description: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for chronic pain.
/glossary/act-therapy.question: What is act?
/glossary/act-therapy.answer: ACT: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is a psychological approach for chronic pain that focuses on living well with pain rather than eliminating it. Growing NICE endorsement for chronic primary pain. Available via NHS Talking Therapies.

/glossary/iapt.title: NHS Talking Therapies: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/iapt.question: What is nhs talking therapies?
/glossary/iapt.answer: NHS Talking Therapies: NHS Talking Therapies (formerly IAPT) provides free CBT, counselling and mindfulness-based therapy for adults with anxiety, depression and chronic pain. Self-referral online in most areas. Waiting times variable.

/glossary/nsaid-topical.title: Topical NSAID: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/nsaid-topical.description: NSAID applied as gel or cream to the skin.
/glossary/nsaid-topical.question: What is topical nsaid?
/glossary/nsaid-topical.answer: Topical NSAID: Topical NSAIDs (ibuprofen gel, diclofenac gel) are applied to the skin over a painful joint. NICE first-line for hand and knee OA — comparable pain relief to oral NSAIDs but far lower systemic risk.

/glossary/capsaicin.title: Capsaicin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/capsaicin.question: What is capsaicin?
/glossary/capsaicin.answer: Capsaicin: Capsaicin cream (from chilli peppers) desensitises pain nerves over 2-4 weeks of regular application. NICE-recommended for OA hand and knee. Available on NHS prescription. Wash hands after use.

/glossary/amitriptyline.title: Amitriptyline: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/amitriptyline.description: A low-dose antidepressant used for pain and sleep.
/glossary/amitriptyline.question: What is amitriptyline?
/glossary/amitriptyline.answer: Amitriptyline: Low-dose amitriptyline (10-25 mg at night) is a common NHS prescription for chronic pain including fibromyalgia and neuropathic pain. Improves sleep and reduces pain sensitivity. Not addictive but takes weeks to work.

/glossary/pregabalin.title: Pregabalin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/pregabalin.description: A drug for nerve pain and fibromyalgia.
/glossary/pregabalin.question: What is pregabalin?
/glossary/pregabalin.answer: Pregabalin: Pregabalin (Lyrica) is used for neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia. Controlled drug in UK — slow to increase, slow to reduce. Side effects: drowsiness, weight gain, dependence risk.

/glossary/gabapentin.title: Gabapentin: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/gabapentin.question: What is gabapentin?
/glossary/gabapentin.answer: Gabapentin: Gabapentin has similar uses to pregabalin (nerve pain, fibromyalgia). Also a controlled drug in the UK. Cheaper than pregabalin. Titrated up over weeks; withdrawal must be gradual.

/glossary/codeine.title: Codeine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/codeine.question: What is codeine?
/glossary/codeine.answer: Codeine: Codeine is a weak opioid, often combined with paracetamol (co-codamol). Constipation is universal; addiction risk with regular use. NICE increasingly cautions against long-term opioid use in chronic non-cancer pain.

/glossary/tramadol.title: Tramadol: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/tramadol.question: What is tramadol?
/glossary/tramadol.answer: Tramadol: Tramadol is a controlled painkiller for moderate pain. Interacts with many antidepressants and can lower seizure threshold. Long-term use in chronic pain is discouraged by current NHS guidance.

/glossary/morphine.title: Morphine: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/morphine.description: A strong opioid, rarely used long-term in arthritis.
/glossary/morphine.question: What is morphine?
/glossary/morphine.answer: Morphine: Strong opioids like morphine are rarely used in chronic arthritis because evidence for long-term benefit is poor and risks (dependence, falls, respiratory depression) are high. Occasionally used short-term for severe flares or post-op.

/glossary/epidural.title: Epidural: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/epidural.description: Injection of drugs into the spinal space.
/glossary/epidural.question: What is epidural?
/glossary/epidural.answer: Epidural: Epidural steroid injections deliver anti-inflammatory drugs to the spine for radiculopathy (nerve root pain). NICE recommends caution — some benefit for acute severe sciatica, limited role in chronic back pain.

/glossary/facet-joint-injection.title: Facet joint injection: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/facet-joint-injection.description: Steroid injection into small spine joints.
/glossary/facet-joint-injection.question: What is facet joint injection?
/glossary/facet-joint-injection.answer: Facet joint injection: Facet joint injections deliver local anaesthetic and steroid to the small joints at the back of the spine. Used for suspected facet-mediated back pain. Evidence for lasting benefit is mixed.

/glossary/radiofrequency-denervation.title: Radiofrequency denervation: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/radiofrequency-denervation.description: Nerve ablation for chronic back pain.
/glossary/radiofrequency-denervation.question: What is radiofrequency denervation?
/glossary/radiofrequency-denervation.answer: Radiofrequency denervation: Radiofrequency denervation heats specific nerves to disrupt pain signals from spinal facet joints. Considered by NICE for carefully selected patients with confirmed facet-joint pain who haven't responded to other treatments.

/glossary/spinal-fusion.title: Spinal fusion: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/spinal-fusion.description: Surgery joining two or more vertebrae together.
/glossary/spinal-fusion.question: What is spinal fusion?
/glossary/spinal-fusion.answer: Spinal fusion: Spinal fusion joins two or more vertebrae together to stop movement causing pain. Considered for specific structural problems (severe instability, deformity). Not a routine treatment for chronic non-specific back pain.

/glossary/prolotherapy.title: Prolotherapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/prolotherapy.description: Injection of irritant solutions to promote healing.
/glossary/prolotherapy.question: What is prolotherapy?
/glossary/prolotherapy.answer: Prolotherapy: Prolotherapy injects irritant solutions (often dextrose) around tendons or joints to stimulate healing. Evidence is preliminary and mixed. Not routinely available on NHS. Sometimes offered privately for chronic joint pain.

/glossary/prp.title: PRP: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/prp.question: What is prp?
/glossary/prp.answer: PRP: PRP (platelet-rich plasma) injections use concentrated platelets from your own blood to promote tissue healing. Evidence for arthritis is emerging but not strong enough for routine NHS use. Common in private sports medicine.

/glossary/stem-cell.title: Stem cell therapy: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/stem-cell.question: What is stem cell therapy?
/glossary/stem-cell.answer: Stem cell therapy: Stem cell therapy for arthritis remains experimental. Regulatory framework is tight. Beware of overseas clinics making strong claims. UK approved treatments are limited to specific research settings.

/glossary/weight-loss-arthritis.title: Weight loss for arthritis: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/weight-loss-arthritis.description: Losing weight to reduce joint load.
/glossary/weight-loss-arthritis.question: What is weight loss for arthritis?
/glossary/weight-loss-arthritis.answer: Weight loss for arthritis: Weight loss of 5-10% substantially reduces knee OA pain. Every 1 kg lost cuts knee load by about 4 kg during walking. Combine with strength work to protect muscle mass.

/glossary/bmi.title: BMI: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/bmi.description: Body mass index, a rough weight-for-height measure.
/glossary/bmi.question: What is bmi?
/glossary/bmi.answer: BMI: BMI is weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared. Rough guide only — doesn't distinguish muscle from fat. NHS categories: <18.5 underweight, 18.5-24.9 healthy, 25-29.9 overweight, 30+ obese.

/glossary/pain-scale.title: Pain scale (0-10): Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/pain-scale.question: What is pain scale (0-10)?
/glossary/pain-scale.answer: Pain scale (0-10): The 0-10 numeric pain rating is used in NHS clinics to track pain over time. 0 = no pain, 10 = worst imaginable. Useful for consultation, less useful for diagnosis (subjective).

/glossary/das28-remission.title: DAS28 remission: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/das28-remission.description: A DAS28 score under 2.6 indicating minimal RA activity.
/glossary/das28-remission.question: What is das28 remission?
/glossary/das28-remission.answer: DAS28 remission: DAS28 < 2.6 is the standard definition of RA remission. Achievable in around half of people on early aggressive treatment. Goal of modern RA management.

/glossary/shared-decision-making.title: Shared decision-making: Meaning & Explanation | Arthritis Glossary
/glossary/shared-decision-making.description: Doctors and patients agreeing treatment together.
/glossary/shared-decision-making.question: What is shared decision-making?
/glossary/shared-decision-making.answer: Shared decision-making: Shared decision-making is a formal NHS approach where clinicians present options and patients contribute values and preferences to reach a treatment plan. Especially important in arthritis where multiple options fit different lifestyles.

/glossary.title: Arthritis Glossary: 110+ UK Terms Explained
/glossary.description: Free UK glossary of arthritis, MSK and rheumatology terms — DMARDs, biologics, ESR, CRP, DAS28 and more, in plain English.
/glossary.question: What arthritis and rheumatology terms should I know?
/glossary.answer: Living With Arthritis UK's plain-English glossary covers 110+ terms across rheumatology, musculoskeletal medicine, treatment, imaging, benefits and self-management — from DMARDs and biologics through DAS28, HLA-B27, sarcopenia and frailty. Every term is medically reviewed and linked to related conditions and guides so you can quickly understand your diagnosis, appointment letters or research articles.

/pets/arthritis-in-dogs.title: Arthritis in Dogs: Signs, Treatment & Daily Care | Living With Arthritis UK
/pets/arthritis-in-dogs.description: Around 80% of dogs over 8 show signs of arthritis. Learn the early warning signs, what your vet can offer (from supplements to Librela), and simple home chan...
/pets/arthritis-in-dogs.breadcrumb: Arthritis in Dogs: Signs, Treatment & Daily Care
/pets/arthritis-in-dogs.question: Which dog breeds get arthritis most?
/pets/arthritis-in-dogs.answer: Around 80% of dogs over 8 show signs of arthritis. Learn the early warning signs, what your vet can offer (from supplements to Librela), and simple home changes that make a big difference. Dogs hide pain well. Look for: slowing on walks, hesitating at stairs or the car boot, stiffness after rest that eases with movement, licking one joint, reluctance to jump on the sofa, and irritability when touched. Limping is a late sign — by the time a dog visibly limps, arthritis is usually well established.

faqs.q: Which dog breeds get arthritis most?
faqs.a: Labradors, Golden Retrievers, German Shepherds, Rottweilers and other large breeds are most affected, plus long-backed breeds like Dachshunds. But any dog can develop arthritis, especially after joint injury or with excess weight.

faqs.q: Should I walk my arthritic dog less?
faqs.a: No — movement keeps joints healthy. Switch to shorter, more frequent, consistent walks on soft ground. Avoid ball-chasing and sudden twisting games, which spike joint load.

faqs.q: Is Librela worth it?
faqs.a: Many UK owners report significant improvement. It's a monthly vet-administered injection (roughly £50-80/month). Discuss with your vet whether your dog is a good candidate — response varies.

/pets/arthritis-in-cats.title: Arthritis in Cats: The Silent Condition | Living With Arthritis UK
/pets/arthritis-in-cats.description: Up to 90% of cats over 12 have arthritic changes on X-ray, yet most are never diagnosed — cats mask pain superbly. Here's how to spot it and what genuinely h...
/pets/arthritis-in-cats.breadcrumb: Arthritis in Cats: The Silent Condition
/pets/arthritis-in-cats.question: How do I know if my cat is in pain?
/pets/arthritis-in-cats.answer: Up to 90% of cats over 12 have arthritic changes on X-ray, yet most are never diagnosed — cats mask pain superbly. Here's how to spot it and what genuinely helps. Cats don't limp the way dogs do — they modify behaviour instead. A cat with sore joints jumps less, climbs less, grooms less (look for a scurfy or matted coat over the back and hips), sleeps more, and may start missing the litter tray because climbing in hurts. Owners often put this down to 'just ageing'. It's usually pain, and it's treatable.

faqs.q: How do I know if my cat is in pain?
faqs.a: Watch behaviour, not limping: reduced jumping, less grooming, hiding more, litter tray accidents, and irritability when stroked over the back or hips are the classic signs.

faqs.q: What is Solensia?
faqs.a: A monthly antibody injection licensed in the UK for feline arthritis pain — the cat version of the dog drug Librela. Many owners see improved jumping and activity within weeks. Discuss suitability with your vet.

faqs.q: Can indoor cats get arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes. Age, genetics and weight matter more than lifestyle. Indoor cats are often heavier, which increases risk.

/pets/arthritis-in-horses.title: Arthritis in Horses: Managing Joints for a Longer Ridden Life | Living With Arthritis UK
/pets/arthritis-in-horses.description: Degenerative joint disease is the leading cause of early retirement in UK horses. Early management — footcare, surfaces, warm-up and vet support — keeps hors...
/pets/arthritis-in-horses.breadcrumb: Arthritis in Horses: Managing Joints for a Longer Ridden Life
/pets/arthritis-in-horses.question: Can an arthritic horse still be ridden?
/pets/arthritis-in-horses.answer: Degenerative joint disease is the leading cause of early retirement in UK horses. Early management — footcare, surfaces, warm-up and vet support — keeps horses comfortable for years longer. Early equine arthritis shows as stiffness that improves with work ('warming out of it'), shortened stride, reluctance on one rein, bunny-hopping into canter, fidgeting for the farrier, or heat and mild filling around a joint after work. Hocks, coffin joints and fetlocks are most commonly affected.

faqs.q: Can an arthritic horse still be ridden?
faqs.a: Usually yes — appropriate, consistent, correctly warmed-up work generally helps rather than harms. Your vet can advise the right level for your horse's joints.

faqs.q: Is box rest good for arthritis?
faqs.a: Generally no. Unlike acute injuries, arthritic joints stiffen with immobility. Most arthritic horses do best with maximum turnout and steady gentle movement.

faqs.q: What age do horses get arthritis?
faqs.a: It's most common from mid-teens onward, but competition horses can show joint changes from as young as 8-10. Early management makes the biggest difference.

/pets/arthritis-in-llamas-and-alpacas.title: Arthritis in Llamas & Alpacas: A Practical Owner's Guide | Living With Arthritis UK
/pets/arthritis-in-llamas-and-alpacas.description: Camelids are stoic animals that hide lameness until it's advanced. Learn the subtle signs of joint disease in llamas and alpacas and the husbandry changes th...
/pets/arthritis-in-llamas-and-alpacas.breadcrumb: Arthritis in Llamas & Alpacas: A Practical Owner's Guide
/pets/arthritis-in-llamas-and-alpacas.question: How long do llamas and alpacas live with arthritis?
/pets/arthritis-in-llamas-and-alpacas.answer: Camelids are stoic animals that hide lameness until it's advanced. Learn the subtle signs of joint disease in llamas and alpacas and the husbandry changes that keep them comfortable. Llamas and alpacas rarely show obvious lameness until joint disease is advanced. Earlier clues: spending more time cushed (lying down), rising slowly or awkwardly, lagging behind the herd, reduced range while grazing, weight shifting at the standing rest, and reluctance on slopes or rough ground. Older animals and those with previous limb injuries are most at risk.

faqs.q: How long do llamas and alpacas live with arthritis?
faqs.a: With good management many live comfortably into their late teens or twenties. Weight control, footcare and dry footing make the biggest difference.

faqs.q: Should I isolate an arthritic alpaca?
faqs.a: No — camelids are herd animals and isolation causes significant stress. Keep them with at least one calm companion, and manage feeding so they aren't pushed off hay.

/pets/senior-pet-exercise-guide.title: Exercise for Arthritic Pets: Little and Often Wins | Living With Arthritis UK
/pets/senior-pet-exercise-guide.description: The single most common mistake owners make is weekend-warrior exercise. Here's how to build a joint-friendly movement routine for dogs, cats and horses alike
/pets/senior-pet-exercise-guide.breadcrumb: Exercise for Arthritic Pets: Little and Often Wins
/pets/senior-pet-exercise-guide.question: Is hydrotherapy worth it for dogs?
/pets/senior-pet-exercise-guide.answer: The single most common mistake owners make is weekend-warrior exercise. Here's how to build a joint-friendly movement routine for dogs, cats and horses alike. Consistent, moderate, frequent movement — never boom and bust. For dogs: three short walks daily beats one long weekend hike. For cats: several short play sessions with a wand toy at ground level. For horses: daily turnout plus regular gentle ridden or in-hand work. Two days of soreness after activity means it was too much; scale back and rebuild gradually.

faqs.q: Is hydrotherapy worth it for dogs?
faqs.a: For many arthritic dogs, yes — it builds muscle that protects joints without impact. UK sessions cost £25-45; some insurers cover it on vet referral.

faqs.q: My cat won't 'exercise' — what can I do?
faqs.a: Cats exercise through play. Two or three 5-minute sessions with a wand toy kept at ground level maintain joint movement without jumping strain.

/pets/pet-weight-and-joint-health.title: Pet Weight & Joint Health: The Treatment Owners Control | Living With Arthritis UK
/pets/pet-weight-and-joint-health.description: Excess weight is the most powerful — and most fixable — driver of arthritis pain in pets. A practical guide to body condition scoring and safe weight loss fo...
/pets/pet-weight-and-joint-health.breadcrumb: Pet Weight & Joint Health: The Treatment Owners Control
/pets/pet-weight-and-joint-health.question: How fast should my dog lose weight?
/pets/pet-weight-and-joint-health.answer: Excess weight is the most powerful — and most fixable — driver of arthritis pain in pets. A practical guide to body condition scoring and safe weight loss for dogs, cats, horses and camelids. In dogs, studies show weight loss of 6-9% of body weight measurably reduces lameness — an effect comparable to starting an NSAID. The mechanics are simple: less load per stride, thousands of strides per day. The same principle holds for cats, horses and camelids.

faqs.q: How fast should my dog lose weight?
faqs.a: About 1-2% of body weight per week. A 30 kg Labrador losing 300-600 g weekly will reach a 4 kg target in roughly 2-3 months.

faqs.q: What's the easiest first step?
faqs.a: Measure meals with digital scales instead of a scoop, and swap treats for part of the daily food ration or vegetables like carrot (dogs). Measuring alone typically cuts 10-20% of calories.

/pets/home-adaptations-for-arthritic-pet.title: Home Adaptations for Arthritic Pets: 15 Cheap Changes That Work | Living With Arthritis UK
/pets/home-adaptations-for-arthritic-pet.description: Ramps, rugs, raised bowls and warm beds — small changes around the home dramatically reduce daily joint strain for arthritic dogs and cats.
/pets/home-adaptations-for-arthritic-pet.breadcrumb: Home Adaptations for Arthritic Pets: 15 Cheap Changes That Work
/pets/home-adaptations-for-arthritic-pet.question: What single change helps most?
/pets/home-adaptations-for-arthritic-pet.answer: Ramps, rugs, raised bowls and warm beds — small changes around the home dramatically reduce daily joint strain for arthritic dogs and cats. Slipping on laminate or tile is both painful and dangerous for arthritic pets. Lay non-slip runners along main routes, add a mat where your pet eats and drinks, and keep claws and foot fur trimmed for grip. Toe grips (small rubber rings for dog claws) help dogs that still slip.

faqs.q: What single change helps most?
faqs.a: For dogs: non-slip flooring on their main routes. For cats: a low-entry litter tray on every floor. Both remove dozens of painful movements per day.

faqs.q: Are heated beds safe for pets?
faqs.a: Yes, if designed for pets with a thermostat and chew-safe cable. They're particularly loved by arthritic cats and thin senior dogs in winter.

/pets/when-to-see-the-vet-pet-arthritis.title: Pet Arthritis: When to See the Vet (Red Flags) | Living With Arthritis UK

/pets/when-to-see-the-vet-pet-arthritis.question: Is limping ever an emergency?
/pets/when-to-see-the-vet-pet-arthritis.answer: Most pet arthritis can be managed at a routine appointment — but some signs need urgent attention. Know the difference. Your pet is gradually stiffer after rest, slower on walks, jumping less, grooming less (cats), or you've noticed two or more changes on the home checks in our species guides. Gradual-onset signs suit a planned consultation where your vet can examine properly and build a stepped plan.

faqs.q: Is limping ever an emergency?
faqs.a: Sudden non-weight-bearing lameness, a hot swollen joint, or lameness with a wound or after trauma needs same-day veterinary attention. Gradual mild stiffness suits a routine appointment.

faqs.q: Can I get help with vet costs in the UK?
faqs.a: PDSA and Blue Cross offer subsidised care for owners on qualifying benefits. Many practices offer payment plans, and pet insurance often covers arthritis treatment if the policy predates the diagnosis.

/pets.question: Can pets get arthritis?
/pets.answer: Yes — arthritis is extremely common in pets. Around 80% of dogs over 8 and up to 90% of cats over 12 show arthritic changes, and it's the leading cause of early retirement in UK horses. Living With Arthritis UK's pet hub covers signs, veterinary treatments (including Librela for dogs and Solensia for cats), weight management, joint-friendly exercise and home adaptations for dogs, cats, horses, llamas and alpacas. One rule above all: never give pets human painkillers — paracetamol and ibuprofen are toxic to dogs and cats.

faqs.q: What pets get arthritis?
faqs.a: Dogs, cats, horses, llamas, alpacas and rabbits all commonly develop arthritis, especially with age, excess weight or previous joint injury.

faqs.q: Can I give my pet human painkillers?
faqs.a: Never. Paracetamol and ibuprofen are toxic to dogs and cats — paracetamol can be fatal to a cat in one dose. Only use medication prescribed by your vet.
